Multi-Capacity Online Assortment Optimization with Consecutive Stays under Markov Chain Choice

Hongbin Zhang    Yanzhi Li    Woonghee Tim Huh
Abstract

We study online assortment optimization under Markov chain choice and independent Bernoulli arrivals, with each period’s request type known in advance. Each product may have multiple interchangeable physical copies, and each booking reserves consecutive service slots on a single copy. Customers choose among products, while the platform assigns purchases to feasible copies. We develop a sales-based relaxation that upper-bounds the optimal online revenue and use it to design a policy with two components: independent sampling and purchase–update coupling. We generate independent copy proposals and make a product eligible whenever at least one of its copies proposes. A general revenue-extraction bound for random candidate sets with independent product inclusions shows that optimizing over eligible products recovers at least half of each period’s relaxation revenue benchmark in expectation. A purchase–update coupling reproduces the interval flows through independent virtual copy updates while preserving physical feasibility. Under general Markov chain choice, the policy uses a random gate to make the coupling feasible: it offers the selected assortment with probability 1−1/e1-1/e and the empty assortment otherwise. No gate is needed under multinomial logit (MNL) choice.

The resulting policies achieve approximation ratios of (1−1/e)/2(1-1/e)/2 and 1/21/2, respectively, relative to the optimal nonanticipative online policy, independently of product capacities. When outside-option attractiveness is zero in every period, the same ungated MNL policy achieves a 1−1/e1-1/e guarantee. Both policies admit exact implementations in expected polynomial time. In the single-copy MNL setting, our policy improves the guarantee of Hu and Wu (2026) from 0.2710.271 to 1/21/2 under the same arrival convention. The 1/21/2 static extraction factor and the 1−1/e1-1/e uniform scalar-gate factor are separately sharp, and the 1/21/2 MNL guarantee is tight for the proposed policy.

1 Introduction

Advance booking changes the nature of capacity. In our setting, a sale does not simply remove one interchangeable unit from an inventory pool; it reserves a particular physical unit for the entire requested service interval, with the assignment fixed irrevocably at booking. In high-speed rail, for example, an accepted itinerary may require immediate and irrevocable assignment to a single seat. Having an available seat on each leg is not sufficient: the same seat must be available on all requested legs (Zhu et al. 2023). Similar requirements arise in hotels, vehicle-rental companies, and other reservation systems when a booking must be fulfilled by the same room or asset throughout the requested stay. These requirements call for tracking each physical unit’s availability across service slots (Rusmevichientong et al. 2023).

The physical unit used to fulfill a booking, however, is often not the alternative chosen by the customer. A rail passenger may choose a seating class, while the firm assigns a specific seat within that class. A related form of fulfillment flexibility appears in flexible-product models, which allow the seller to assign a customer to one of several specified alternatives after purchase (Gallego et al. 2004). We call each customer-facing category a product and its individual physical units copies. Copies of the same product are interchangeable from the customer’s perspective, but the firm must distinguish them for assignment and capacity accounting.

This product–copy distinction matters for both feasibility and customer choice. With existing assignments fixed, tracking only the number of available copies in each service slot may suggest that a request is feasible even when no single copy can fulfill it. For example, one seat may be available on the first leg of a journey and another on the second, even though neither is available for both legs. Displaying physical copies as separate alternatives without a corresponding reformulation of the choice model can change product purchase probabilities. We therefore model customer choice at the product level while tracking individual copies for feasibility and assignment.

Consecutive stays also complicate the evolution of each copy’s availability. Reserving an interior portion of a free interval splits it into two disjoint blocks, so the feasibility of later requests depends on which service slots remain free, not merely how many. This differs from standard inventory models, which track remaining stock, and from many reusable-resource models, which summarize availability through release times or counts of available units. In our setting, booking periods and service slots play distinct roles: requests arrive sequentially during the booking horizon, while each accepted reservation occupies an interval of service slots on its assigned copy. Once reserved, those slots remain unavailable on that copy for the rest of the booking horizon.

We adopt the fixed-type Bernoulli-arrival convention of Hu and Wu (2026) over a finite booking horizon. Each period has at most one potential customer, and arrivals are independent across periods. The arrival probabilities, requested intervals, revenues, and choice parameters for all periods are known before the booking horizon begins and may vary across periods. Arrival and choice outcomes are observed only as they occur. Before observing the arrival outcome in each period, the platform selects an assortment of products with feasible copies and offers it if the customer arrives. Each purchase is assigned to a single copy available throughout the requested interval. We model customer substitution using the Markov chain choice model of Blanchet et al. (2016). The chain is defined over customer-visible products and the outside option, and the customer’s path stops upon first reaching an offered product or the outside option. This model includes multinomial logit (MNL) choice with positive outside-option attractiveness and allows richer substitution patterns. We treat MNL with zero outside-option attractiveness separately.

The closest related work is Hu and Wu (2026), whose fixed-type Bernoulli model is included in our setting when each product has one copy and choice follows MNL. Building on their interval-flow relaxation and proposal-discarding framework, we extend the analysis to general Markov chain choice and multiple copies per product. The main challenge is to coordinate product-level customer choice with copy-level proposals and virtual updates.

Our benchmark is the expected revenue of the optimal nonanticipative online policy. Like our algorithm, this policy knows the model primitives but observes arrival and choice outcomes only as they occur. The benchmark ranges over all feasible history-dependent policies, without computational restrictions. Approximation guarantees for efficient policies relative to this benchmark are often called philosopher inequalities, whereas prophet inequalities use a clairvoyant offline benchmark (Papadimitriou et al. 2024, Huang et al. 2024). We construct policies that admit exact implementations in expected polynomial time and achieve approximation guarantees of (1−1/e)/2(1-1/e)/2 under general Markov chain choice and 1/21/2 under MNL, relative to this benchmark and independently of product capacities.

1.1 Literature Review

Our work relates to four research streams: (i) choice-based revenue management, (ii) flexible assignment and reusable resources, (iii) interval scheduling and advance booking, and (iv) online approximation and rounding.

(i) Choice-Based Revenue Management. Classical network revenue management studies how to allocate limited capacity among products with fixed resource requirements, balancing current revenue against the value of preserving capacity for future demand (Gallego and van Ryzin 1997, Talluri and van Ryzin 1998). Choice-based models incorporate customer substitution by allowing demand to depend on the assortment offered. Talluri and van Ryzin (2004) study revenue management under a general discrete-choice model. Liu and van Ryzin (2008) analyze a choice-based linear programming formulation for network revenue management, and Gallego et al. (2015) develop a sales-based formulation that incorporates customer choice into capacity allocation.

Related work examines how assortments should vary across customers and over time. Golrezaei et al. (2014) study real-time personalized assortments, while Aouad et al. (2018) develop greedy-like algorithms for assortment planning under MNL choice. Ma and Simchi-Levi (2020) analyze online algorithms for assortment and pricing decisions, and Ma et al. (2021) study the performance of price and assortment calendars fixed in advance.

Within this literature, the Markov chain choice model represents substitution through transitions among product states (Blanchet et al. 2016). Feldman and Topaloglu (2017) develop LP formulations for assortment optimization under this model and an equivalent compact relaxation for network revenue management. They also provide a procedure for recovering an optimal assortment mixture. Désir et al. (2020) develop algorithms for constrained assortment optimization under the same choice model. Our analysis uses the continuation structure of Markov paths to establish a lower bound on the expected revenue from optimizing over a random candidate set in which products are included independently.

(ii) Flexible Assignment and Reusable Resources. Flexible-product models allow the seller to assign a customer to one of several specified alternatives after purchase (Gallego et al. 2004). Our model involves a related form of fulfillment flexibility: the customer purchases a product, and the seller assigns the booking to one of its interchangeable physical copies.

A related literature studies assortment, pricing, and allocation for resources that become available again after service completion. Rusmevichientong et al. (2020) study dynamic assortment optimization with random usage durations. Lei and Jasin (2020) analyze dynamic pricing with deterministic service durations, with extensions to heterogeneous durations and advance reservations. Gong et al. (2022) study online assortment optimization with reusable resources, while Baek and Ma (2022) develop approximation methods for network revenue management with resource reuse. Further work considers Bayesian online assortment optimization (Feng et al. 2024) and online allocation under adversarial requests (Goyal et al. 2025).

Our setting combines Markov substitution among products with the requirement that each booking be fulfilled by a single physical copy throughout the requested service interval. Accepted reservations remain fixed throughout the booking horizon, and the feasibility of subsequent requests depends on which service slots remain free on each copy. The policy must therefore coordinate assortment and assignment decisions using each copy’s free-slot set.

(iii) Interval Scheduling and Advance Booking. Classical fixed-interval scheduling assigns jobs with prescribed start and end times to machines so that no two jobs overlap on the same machine (Kolen et al. 2007, Kovalyov et al. 2007). Chawla et al. (2019) study Bayesian online allocation with interval demand. In revenue-management applications, Zhu et al. (2023) impose the assign-to-seat requirement that an accepted rail itinerary use the same physical seat throughout the journey. Rusmevichientong et al. (2023) study assortment decisions for heterogeneous unit-capacity resources requested over service intervals. These studies highlight the need to track availability on individual resources when each request must be fulfilled by the same resource throughout its service interval.

The closest methodological reference is Hu and Wu (2026), who develop interval-flow relaxations and use virtual resource states with proposal discarding for consecutive-stay revenue management. Their choice-based model uses MNL and treats each physical resource as a customer-facing alternative. Under fixed-type Bernoulli arrivals, this model is included in our MNL specialization with one physical copy per product. They also consider general arrivals with random request types. Their MNL policy samples virtual resource updates after observing the customer’s choice. This construction ensures that the purchased resource is updated and recovers the prescribed independent update law after averaging over the choice outcome.

We build on this framework to accommodate general Markov chain choice and multiple copies per product. Our static analysis establishes a revenue-extraction bound for random candidate sets in which products are included independently. For dynamic implementation, we characterize coupling feasibility through necessary and sufficient Hall-type coverage conditions. A priority-rule representation and copy-level lifting then generate the required virtual updates. Under fixed-type Bernoulli arrivals, our MNL policy improves the approximation guarantee of Hu and Wu (2026) from 0.2710.271 to 1/21/2. This improvement holds even with one copy per product and, in that setting, follows from the stronger static revenue-extraction bound. Table 1.1 summarizes the comparison.

(iv) Online Approximation and Rounding. Our approximation guarantees use the optimal online benchmark described above. The guarantees of Hu et al. (2026) concern inventory depletion and do not directly apply to our setting, where feasibility depends on each physical copy’s availability throughout the requested service interval. In online stochastic matching, relaxation marginals guide randomized proposals, while discarding and dependent rounding help preserve feasibility and control dependence (Braverman et al. 2022, Braverman et al. 2025). In our setting, implementing the relaxation requires tracking each copy’s free service slots and assigning each purchase to a copy available throughout the requested interval.

Contention-resolution schemes similarly transform fractional or independently sampled solutions into feasible discrete outcomes (Chekuri et al. 2014, Kashaev and Santiago 2023, Sergeev 2024). Our implementation must also preserve a prescribed joint law for virtual copy updates. After observing the purchase outcome, the policy generates updates that include at least one proposed copy of the purchased product whenever a purchase occurs. Conditional on the current virtual states and proposals, averaging over purchase outcomes must recover the prescribed joint law of independent copy updates. We characterize coupling feasibility through Hall-type coverage conditions and use a priority-rule decomposition to construct the conditional sampler.

1.2 Main Results and Contributions

Our main contributions are a general revenue-extraction bound under Markov chain choice and approximation guarantees for consecutive-stay systems with arbitrary product capacities.

  • •

    A general revenue-extraction bound under Markov chain choice. We establish a general bound on the expected revenue from optimizing over a random candidate set with independent product inclusions, relative to the expected revenue of an arbitrary randomized benchmark assortment (Theorem 2). We express the bound in terms of candidate-inclusion probabilities and benchmark purchase probabilities normalized by singleton purchase probabilities. Our analysis does not require candidate-inclusion probabilities to sum to at most one or match the benchmark’s product-inclusion probabilities. We prove the bound using a continuation decomposition of Markov paths and simultaneous independent thinning of the candidate set.

    The result applies beyond the consecutive-stay setting. Applying it to our proposal mechanism, we show that optimizing over products with at least one proposing copy recovers at least half of each period’s relaxation revenue in expectation, for arbitrary copy multiplicities.

  • •

    Purchase–update coupling for dynamic implementation. We characterize when a purchase outcome can be coupled with prescribed independent Bernoulli product updates so that every purchased product receives an update. Necessary and sufficient Hall-type coverage inequalities describe the feasible purchase distributions. Using the classical greedy representation of the resulting coverage polymatroid (Edmonds 2003), we construct a priority-rule decomposition and a sampler conditional on the observed purchase outcome.

    We lift these product updates to individual proposed copies, assigning every purchase to a copy selected for a virtual update. Conditional on the current virtual states, proposals, and selected assortment, averaging over purchase outcomes recovers the prescribed joint law of independent copy updates. Other updated copies undergo only virtual discards and consume no physical capacity. This construction preserves the relaxation’s interval marginals and independence across virtual copies at the beginning of each booking period, while keeping virtual availability within actual availability.

    Under general Markov chain choice, in each nonterminal period, the policy offers the selected assortment with probability 1−1/e1-1/e and the empty assortment otherwise. This gate ensures coupling feasibility. Combining this implementation with static revenue extraction gives a (1−1/e)/2{(1-1/e)}/{2}-approximation relative to both the relaxation and the optimal nonanticipative online value, for arbitrary product capacities (Theorem 1(i)).

  • •

    An improved MNL guarantee and sharpness results. Under MNL, all Hall-type coupling conditions hold without gating, so dynamic implementation introduces no additional revenue loss. The resulting policy achieves a 1/2{1}/{2}-approximation relative to both benchmarks for arbitrary product capacities (Theorem 1(ii)). Under the common fixed-type Bernoulli-arrival setting, this improves the general MNL guarantee of Hu and Wu (2026) from 0.2710.271 to 1/21/2, even with one copy per product. When the outside option has zero attractiveness in every period, the same policy attains a 1−1/e1-1/e guarantee relative to both benchmarks for arbitrary copy multiplicities, matching their guarantee for this case (Remark 3).

    We establish separate sharpness of the 1/21/2 static extraction factor and the 1−1/e1-1/e uniform scalar-gate factor. The extraction factor is sharp even on one-period, unit-capacity instances with uniquely determined optimal sales flows. These results do not establish tightness of the combined Markov guarantee. Under MNL, one-period instances with one copy per product show that the proposed policy’s revenue ratio relative to the optimal online value approaches 1/21/2, establishing tightness for this policy.

Building on the interval-flow and proposal-discarding framework of Hu and Wu (2026), we use a copy-expanded sales-based linear program (SBLP) that upper-bounds the optimal online value and provides target flows for independent copy proposals. To handle multiple copies, the relaxation combines product-level customer choice with maximal-free-interval marginals for individual copies. Aggregating interchangeable copies yields an equivalent relaxation whose number of interval state and sales-flow variables is independent of the product capacities. A symmetric lift recovers feasible copy-level flows with the same objective value.

2 Model and Benchmark

We introduce the consecutive-stay system with multiple copies per product, specify the customer-choice model, and define the online benchmark. Customers choose among products, while the platform assigns each purchase to a physical copy available throughout the requested service interval.

2.1 Multi-Capacity System and Consecutive Stays

We consider a booking system with TT periods in which the platform selects product assortments and assigns purchases to physical copies. The objective is to maximize total expected revenue over the booking horizon.

Products and physical copies. Let ℳ={1,…,M}\mathcal{M}=\{1,\ldots,M\} denote the set of customer-visible products. Product ii has Ci∈ℤ+C_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} interchangeable physical copies, indexed by c∈[Ci]c\in[C_{i}]. Each copy (i,c)(i,c) can fulfill only product ii. Copies are distinguished solely for capacity accounting and assignment. Regardless of CiC_{i}, product ii appears at most once in an offered assortment. Since at most TT bookings can be accepted over the horizon, replacing CiC_{i} by min⁡{Ci,T}\min\{C_{i},T\} leaves the optimal online value unchanged. We therefore assume Ci≤TC_{i}\leq T without loss of generality.

Service slots and booking periods. Let 𝒩={1,…,N}\mathcal{N}=\{1,\ldots,N\} denote the ordered set of service slots and 𝒯={1,…,T}\mathcal{T}=\{1,\ldots,T\} the set of booking periods. Once a service slot on a copy is reserved, it remains unavailable for the rest of the booking horizon. At the beginning of period tt, let ℱt​i​c⊆𝒩\mathcal{F}_{tic}\subseteq\mathcal{N} denote the free service slots on copy (i,c)(i,c). Initially, every copy is fully available: ℱ1​i​c=𝒩\mathcal{F}_{1ic}=\mathcal{N} for all i∈ℳi\in\mathcal{M} and c∈[Ci]c\in[C_{i}].

Each booking period tt has at most one potential customer, who arrives with probability pt∈(0,1]p_{t}\in(0,1], independently across periods. The customer’s request is for the consecutive service interval It=[ℓt,rt]⊆𝒩I_{t}=[\ell_{t},r_{t}]\subseteq\mathcal{N}, where 1≤ℓt≤rt≤N1\leq\ell_{t}\leq r_{t}\leq N. Arrival and choice outcomes remain uncertain and are observed only as they occur.

Feasibility and sequence of events. Each accepted booking is irrevocably assigned to a single physical copy for its entire requested service interval. Thus, copy (i,c)(i,c) can fulfill the period-tt request if and only if It⊆ℱt​i​cI_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{tic}. 2.2 Markov Chain Choice

2.3 Online Policies, Performance Benchmark, and Main Results

A feasible nonanticipative online policy may use internal randomization to select its period-tt assortment based on the model primitives, the history through period t−1t-1, and the current free-slot sets, without observing current or future arrival and choice realizations. If a purchase occurs, the policy assigns it to a feasible copy of the purchased product. For an instance II, let Πon​(I)\Pi^{\rm on}(I) denote the set of feasible nonanticipative online policies, and let Vπ​(I)V^{\pi}(I) denote the expected revenue earned by policy π∈Πon​(I)\pi\in\Pi^{\rm on}(I). Our performance benchmark is the optimal online value, Von​(I):=supπ∈Πon​(I)Vπ​(I)V^{\rm on}(I):=\sup_{\pi\in\Pi^{\rm on}(I)}V^{\pi}(I).

A booking reserves a consecutive service interval on a single copy, preventing that copy from serving later requests with overlapping service intervals. Customer substitution makes expected revenue depend nonlinearly on the offered assortment. The platform must therefore coordinate assortment and assignment decisions while tracking each copy’s availability. We establish the following approximation guarantees.

Theorem 1 (Multi-capacity approximation guarantees)

Under the fixed-type Bernoulli-arrival model, there exist feasible nonanticipative policies with the following guarantees:

  1. (i)

    Markov chain choice. For every instance II under Markov chain choice, policy πMC\pi_{\rm MC} satisfies

    VπMC​(I)≥1−1/e2​Von​(I)V^{\pi_{\rm MC}}(I)\geq\frac{1-1/e}{2}V^{\rm on}(I) (3)
  2. (ii)

    MNL choice. For every instance II under MNL choice with positive outside-option attractiveness in every period, policy πMNL\pi_{\rm MNL} satisfies

    VπMNL​(I)≥12​Von​(I)V^{\pi_{\rm MNL}}(I)\geq\frac{1}{2}V^{\rm on}(I) (4)

Both policies admit exact implementations in expected time polynomial in T,N,MT,N,M and the size of the model input. The approximation factors are independent of the product capacities.

The policies πMC\pi_{\rm MC} and πMNL\pi_{\rm MNL} are the Markov and MNL versions of Algorithm 1 in Section 7, respectively; their construction and analysis follow below. The next section introduces a relaxation that links copy-level availability to product-level choice probabilities and provides the target flows used to construct these policies.

3 Sales-Based Fluid Relaxation

We first formulate the relaxation and show that its optimal value upper-bounds the optimal online value. We then derive an equivalent aggregate formulation that can be solved efficiently.

3.1 Copy-Expanded SBLP and Its Benchmark Bound

The availability of a physical copy is described by its free-slot set, which can be any subset of 𝒩\mathcal{N}. Tracking its distribution can therefore require up to 2N2^{N} states per copy. Our relaxation decomposes each free-slot set into maximal consecutive intervals and tracks their marginal probabilities without retaining their joint distribution. Related interval-based representations appear in revenue-management and seat-allocation models with interval demand (Rusmevichientong et al. 2023, Zhu et al. 2023) and form the basis of the consecutive-stay relaxation of Hu and Wu (2026).

Recall that ℱt​i​c⊆𝒩\mathcal{F}_{tic}\subseteq\mathcal{N} denotes the free service slots on copy (i,c)(i,c) at the beginning of period tt. For any free-slot set ℱ⊆𝒩\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{N}, an interval [a,b]⊆ℱ[a,b]\subseteq\mathcal{F} is a maximal free interval if it cannot be extended in either direction while remaining in ℱ\mathcal{F}. Its endpoints must therefore satisfy both conditions: a=1a=1 or a−1∉ℱa-1\notin\mathcal{F}, and b=Nb=N or b+1∉ℱb+1\notin\mathcal{F}. We denote this relationship by [a,b]∼ℱ[a,b]\sim\mathcal{F}. For example, the maximal free intervals of ℱ={1,2,3,6,7}\mathcal{F}=\{1,2,3,6,7\} are [1,3][1,3] and [6,7][6,7]. The interval [1,2][1,2] is free but not maximal because slot 33 is also free. Every free-slot set has a unique decomposition into disjoint maximal free intervals.

A copy can fulfill the request It=[ℓt,rt]I_{t}=[\ell_{t},r_{t}] if and only if one of its maximal free intervals contains ItI_{t}. Since these intervals are disjoint, the containing interval is unique whenever it exists. Fulfilling the request from [a,b][a,b] removes ItI_{t}, leaving the left residual interval [a,ℓt−1][a,\ell_{t}-1] when a<ℓta<\ell_{t} and the right residual interval [rt+1,b][r_{t}+1,b] when rt<br_{t}<b. Thus, each sale removes one maximal free interval and creates at most two smaller ones, leaving all other maximal free intervals unchanged.

Let 𝒬:={[a,b]:1≤a≤b≤N}\mathcal{Q}:=\{[a,b]:1\leq a\leq b\leq N\} denote the set of all N⁡(N+1)/2N(N+1)/2 service intervals. For each t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}, i∈ℳi\in\mathcal{M}, c∈[Ci]c\in[C_{i}], and [a,b]∈𝒬[a,b]\in\mathcal{Q}, we introduce nonnegative variables with the following intended probabilistic interpretations:

  • •

    xt​i​c​([a,b])x_{tic}([a,b]) is the probability that [a,b][a,b] is a maximal free interval of copy (i,c)(i,c) at the beginning of period tt.

  • •

    yt​i​c​([a,b])y_{tic}([a,b]) is the joint probability that [a,b][a,b] is a maximal free interval of copy (i,c)(i,c) at the beginning of period tt, the customer arrives and purchases product ii, and the purchase is assigned to this copy and fulfilled from [a,b][a,b].

We remark that a copy may have several maximal free intervals simultaneously, so the events represented by the xx-variables are not mutually exclusive. Under this interpretation, ∑[a,b]∈𝒬xt​i​c​([a,b])\sum_{[a,b]\in\mathcal{Q}}x_{tic}([a,b]) equals the expected number of maximal free intervals on copy (i,c)(i,c) at the beginning of period tt and need not equal one.

Following the sales-based linear programming framework of Gallego et al. (2015), we combine copy-level interval flows with product-level choice variables. For each period tt and assortment S⊆ℳS\subseteq\mathcal{M}, let θt​S≥0\theta_{tS}\geq 0 denote the mixture weight on SS, and let zt​iz_{ti} denote the resulting purchase probability of product ii, conditional on an arrival.

Equations (6)–(8) connect assortment choices to sales. The weights θt​S\theta_{tS} form a distribution over assortments, and zt​iz_{ti} is the corresponding purchase probability conditional on an arrival. The unconditional sales probability pt​zt​ip_{t}z_{ti} is then allocated across copies and intervals through the yy-variables. Equations (10)–(11) describe the evolution and initialization of the interval marginals. The initial condition (11) reflects that every copy is initially free over [1,N][1,N].

3.2 Exact Symmetry Reduction and Tractability

Copies of the same product have identical initial conditions and interval-flow constraints. We therefore aggregate their interval state and sales-flow variables to reduce the size of the relaxation. Define

Aggregation maps every feasible copy-expanded solution to a feasible aggregate solution with the same objective value. Conversely, every feasible aggregate solution admits the symmetric lift

xt​i​c​([a,b])=Xt​i​([a,b])Ci,yt​i​c​([a,b])=Yt​i​([a,b])Ci,c∈[Ci],x_{tic}([a,b])=\frac{X_{ti}([a,b])}{C_{i}},\hskip 20.00003pty_{tic}([a,b])=\frac{Y_{ti}([a,b])}{C_{i}},\hskip 20.00003ptc\in[C_{i}],

with θ\theta and zz unchanged. Each copy’s interval constraints and initial conditions follow by dividing their aggregate counterparts by CiC_{i}. The lifted sales flows sum to the original aggregate flows, preserving both the sales-linking constraints and the objective value. This establishes the following result.

Proposition 2 (Exact symmetry reduction)

The aggregate and copy-expanded SBLP formulations have the same optimal value. The aggregate formulation contains O⁡(T​M​N2)O(TMN^{2}) interval state and sales-flow variables, independently of the product capacities CiC_{i}.

Although aggregation reduces the interval variables, the assortment-mixture variables θt​S\theta_{tS} remain exponential in number. After eliminating zz using (7), the unrestricted dual multipliers αt\alpha_{t} and βt​i\beta_{ti} for (6) and the aggregate form of (8), respectively, yield the constraints

αt≥pt​∑i∈Sβt​i​ϕt​i​(S),t∈𝒯,S⊆ℳ.\alpha_{t}\geq p_{t}\sum_{i\in S}\beta_{ti}\phi_{ti}(S),\hskip 20.00003ptt\in\mathcal{T},\ S\subseteq\mathcal{M}.

Checking these constraints amounts to maximizing their right-hand side for each period. By regularity, it suffices to solve the following problem for eligible products A⊆ℳA\subseteq\mathcal{M} and weights w∈ℝ+Mw\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{M}:

max⁡∑i∈SS⊆A⁡wi​ϕt​i​(S).\max_{S\subseteq A}\sum_{i\in S}w_{i}\phi_{ti}(S). (16)

For dual separation, take A={i∈ℳ:βt​i>0}A=\{i\in\mathcal{M}:\beta_{ti}>0\} and wi=max⁡{βt​i,0}w_{i}=\max\{\beta_{ti},0\}. Products outside AA remain transition states but cannot be offered. This Markov assortment problem can be solved in polynomial time through an optimal-stopping formulation (Blanchet et al. 2016). Together with direct checks of the remaining dual constraints, this oracle allows the constructive ellipsoid method to solve the aggregate SBLP and recover an optimal primal solution without enumerating all assortments (Grötschel et al. 1981).

Let Ctot:=∑i∈ℳCiC_{\rm tot}:=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}C_{i} denote the total number of physical copies. Accounting also for the construction of the symmetric copy-level lift yields the following result.

Proposition 3 (Polynomial solvability of the aggregate relaxation)

An optimal aggregate SBLP solution and its symmetric copy-level lift can be computed in time polynomial in T,N,M,CtotT,N,M,C_{\rm tot} and the size of the model input. The assortment mixture can be represented using at most M+1M+1 positive weights per period.

Through the symmetric lift, we assign identical target flows to copies of the same product. Explicitly representing these flows requires O⁡(T​N2​Ctot)O(TN^{2}C_{\rm tot}) entries. In the online policy, we also track actual and virtual availability separately for each copy. Thus, although aggregation makes the interval-variable count independent of product capacities, constructing the copy-level flows and implementing the policy still depend on CtotC_{\rm tot}. Since Ci≤TC_{i}\leq T, we have Ctot≤M​TC_{\rm tot}\leq MT, so this dependence remains polynomial in the model dimensions. We use these target flows to generate proposals in Section 5. Before presenting that construction, we establish a general revenue-extraction bound for independent candidate sets.

4 Revenue Extraction under Markov Chain Choice

We establish a static revenue bound for independent candidate sets relative to an arbitrary randomized-assortment benchmark. The result is independent of the consecutive-stay setting and will later be applied to the candidate sets generated by our copy-proposal mechanism.

Choice Model and Benchmark. Consider the Markov chain choice model defined in Subsection 2.2, with the time index suppressed. Let ri≥0r_{i}\geq 0 denote the revenue of product ii, and recall its singleton purchase probability ai:=ϕi​({i})a_{i}:=\phi_{i}(\{i\}). Write R⁡(S):=∑i∈Sri​ϕi​(S)R(S):=\sum_{i\in S}r_{i}\phi_{i}(S) for the expected revenue from offering assortment SS, and define f⁡(A):=maxS⊆A⁡R⁡(S)f(A):=\max_{S\subseteq A}R(S) for a candidate set A⊆ℳA\subseteq\mathcal{M}.

Let BB be an arbitrary random benchmark assortment with ℙ⁡(B=S)=θS\mathbb{P}(B=S)=\theta_{S}; its product-inclusion indicators need not be independent. Define the benchmark purchase probabilities as zi:=𝔼⁡[ϕi​(B)]=∑S∋iθS​ϕi​(S)z_{i}:=\mathbb{E}[\phi_{i}(B)]=\sum_{S\ni i}\theta_{S}\phi_{i}(S) and its expected revenue as W:=∑i∈ℳri​ziW:=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}r_{i}z_{i}. We assume W>0W>0; otherwise, the revenue lower bound follows from nonnegativity.

Independent Candidate Sets. Let P⊆ℳP\subseteq\mathcal{M} have mutually independent product-inclusion indicators, with pi:=ℙ⁡(i∈P)p_{i}:=\mathbb{P}(i\in P). Define the normalized benchmark target as ρi:=zi/ai\rho_{i}:=z_{i}/a_{i} when ai>0a_{i}>0, and set ρi:=0\rho_{i}:=0 when ai=0a_{i}=0. Regularity gives 0≤zi≤ai0\leq z_{i}\leq a_{i}, so the latter convention applies only when zi=0z_{i}=0, and 0≤ρi≤10\leq\rho_{i}\leq 1. For a realized candidate set PP, f⁡(P)f(P) is the maximum expected revenue obtainable by offering an assortment contained in PP.

Theorem 2 (Revenue extraction under Markov choice)

For any independent candidate set PP with ℙ⁡(i∈P)=pi\mathbb{P}(i\in P)=p_{i},

𝔼[f(P)]≥(mini:zi>0pipi+ρi​(1−pi))∑i∈ℳrizi.\mathbb{E}[f(P)]\geq\left(\min_{i:z_{i}>0}\frac{p_{i}}{p_{i}+\rho_{i}(1-p_{i})}\right)\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}r_{i}z_{i}. (17)

In particular, if pi≥ρi/(1+ρi)p_{i}\geq\rho_{i}/(1+\rho_{i}) for every product with zi>0z_{i}>0, then 𝔼⁡[f⁡(P)]≥12​∑i∈ℳri​zi\mathbb{E}[f(P)]\geq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}r_{i}z_{i}.

The theorem allows arbitrary inclusion probabilities pi∈[0,1]p_{i}\in[0,1], without requiring their sum to be at most one. Its comparison differs from a standard correlation-gap comparison, which fixes a set function and compares independent and correlated distributions with the same inclusion marginals (Agrawal et al. 2010). Here, the benchmark is 𝔼⁡[R⁡(B)]\mathbb{E}[R(B)], and zi=𝔼⁡[ϕi​(B)]z_{i}=\mathbb{E}[\phi_{i}(B)] records a purchase probability rather than an inclusion probability. The candidate probabilities pip_{i} need not equal either ziz_{i} or Pr⁡(i∈B)\Pr(i\in B). The bound instead connects independent product availability to benchmark purchases through ρi=zi/ai\rho_{i}=z_{i}/a_{i}.

Relation to Hu and Wu (2026). In their analysis of the MNL setting with positive outside-option attractiveness, Hu and Wu (2026) study the corresponding static revenue-extraction problem. In our notation, their proposal mechanism yields pi=ρi=zi/aip_{i}=\rho_{i}=z_{i}/a_{i}, and their analysis establishes 𝔼⁡[f⁡(P)]≥0.271​W\mathbb{E}[f(P)]\geq 0.271W. Their proof combines a convexity bound for offering all low-attractiveness proposals with a tail-probability bound for the best high-attractiveness singleton, optimizing the threshold between the groups.

Theorem 2 gives a unified analysis through a Markov-path decomposition and independent thinning. For the same MNL proposal probabilities pi=ρip_{i}=\rho_{i}, it yields

𝔼[f(P)]≥(mini:zi>012−ρi)W≥12W.\mathbb{E}[f(P)]\geq\left(\min_{i:z_{i}>0}\frac{1}{2-\rho_{i}}\right)W\geq\frac{1}{2}W.

Thus, for the same proposal probabilities, our analysis strengthens the single-period revenue guarantee from 0.271​W0.271W to at least W/2W/2. More generally, the theorem applies to Markov chain choice and allows candidate-inclusion probabilities that differ from the normalized benchmark targets.

4.1 Proof of Theorem 2

The proof has two steps. First, a Markov-path decomposition relates singleton purchase probabilities to the benchmark purchase probabilities. Second, we independently thin the candidate set so that every product attains the same fraction of its benchmark purchase probability. The decomposition shows that a product retained whenever available meets its target whenever all other products remain below theirs. Regularity then allows us to attain all targets simultaneously. Because the thinned assortment is contained in PP, optimizing over PP earns at least its expected revenue.

4.1.1 Markov-Path Decomposition and the Benchmark Bound

Let Z0,Z1,…Z_{0},Z_{1},\ldots follow the underlying Markov chain without stopping at offered products. Define the hitting times Ti:=inf{n≥0:Zn=i}T_{i}:=\inf\{n\geq 0:Z_{n}=i\} and T0:=inf{n≥0:Zn=0}T_{0}:=\inf\{n\geq 0:Z_{n}=0\}. For a chain started from the initial distribution λ\lambda, ai=ℙλ​(Ti<T0)a_{i}=\mathbb{P}_{\lambda}(T_{i}<T_{0}). For a chain started from product jj, write hj​i:=ℙj​(Ti<T0)h_{ji}:=\mathbb{P}_{j}(T_{i}<T_{0}). These continuation probabilities satisfy 0≤hj​i≤10\leq h_{ji}\leq 1 and hi​i=1h_{ii}=1, since hitting times include time zero.

The following decomposition separates paths according to the first offered product they reach, then follows their continuation toward product ii.

Proposition 4 (Markov-path decomposition)

For every product ii and assortment S⊆ℳS\subseteq\mathcal{M},

∑j∈Shj​i​ϕj​(S)≤ai.\sum_{j\in S}h_{ji}\phi_{j}(S)\leq a_{i}.

Equality holds whenever i∈Si\in S.

Proof.

Proof. Let τS:=inf{n≥0:Zn∈S∪{0}}\tau_{S}:=\inf\{n\geq 0:Z_{n}\in S\cup\{0\}\}. Transience of the product states makes τS\tau_{S} finite almost surely. For each j∈Sj\in S, define

Ej:={ZτS=j,Zn=i for some n with τS≤n<T0}.E_{j}:=\left\{Z_{\tau_{S}}=j,\hskip 10.00002ptZ_{n}=i\text{ for some }n\text{ with }\tau_{S}\leq n<T_{0}\right\}.

The strong Markov property gives ℙλ​(Ej)=ϕj​(S)​hj​i\mathbb{P}_{\lambda}(E_{j})=\phi_{j}(S)h_{ji}. The events EjE_{j} are mutually disjoint and contained in {Ti<T0}\{T_{i}<T_{0}\}. Hence,

∑j∈Shj​i​ϕj​(S)=ℙλ​(⋃j∈SEj)≤ℙλ​(Ti<T0)=ai.\sum_{j\in S}h_{ji}\phi_{j}(S)=\mathbb{P}_{\lambda}\!\left(\bigcup_{j\in S}E_{j}\right)\leq\mathbb{P}_{\lambda}(T_{i}<T_{0})=a_{i}.

If i∈Si\in S, every path with Ti<T0T_{i}<T_{0} satisfies τS≤Ti\tau_{S}\leq T_{i} and first reaches some j∈Sj\in S. It therefore belongs to exactly one event EjE_{j}, giving ⋃j∈SEj={Ti<T0}\bigcup_{j\in S}E_{j}=\{T_{i}<T_{0}\} and proving equality. For S=∅S=\varnothing, the inequality is immediate. ■\blacksquare ∎

Averaging this decomposition over the benchmark assortment gives a bound expressed directly in terms of its purchase probabilities.

Lemma 1 (Benchmark continuation bound)

For every product ii,

∑j≠ihj​i​zj≤ai−zi.\sum_{j\neq i}h_{ji}z_{j}\leq a_{i}-z_{i}.
Proof.

Proof. Apply Proposition 4 to each realization of BB and take expectations. Since ϕj​(B)=0\phi_{j}(B)=0 when j∉Bj\notin B and hi​i=1h_{ii}=1,

zi+∑j≠ihj​i​zj=∑j∈ℳhj​i​𝔼​[ϕj​(B)]≤ai.z_{i}+\sum_{j\neq i}h_{ji}z_{j}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{M}}h_{ji}\mathbb{E}[\phi_{j}(B)]\leq a_{i}.

Rearranging proves the claim. No independence assumption on the benchmark assortment is needed. ■\blacksquare ∎

4.1.2 Independent Thinning to Match the Purchase Targets

Let I+:={i∈ℳ:zi>0}I^{+}:=\{i\in\mathcal{M}:z_{i}>0\}. If pi=0p_{i}=0 for some i∈I+i\in I^{+}, the coefficient in (17) is zero and the theorem is immediate. We therefore assume pi>0p_{i}>0 for every i∈I+i\in I^{+}, and set

ϑ:=mini∈I+⁡pipi+ρi​(1−pi).\vartheta:=\min_{i\in I^{+}}\frac{p_{i}}{p_{i}+\rho_{i}(1-p_{i})}.

Since 0<ρi≤10<\rho_{i}\leq 1 on I+I^{+}, we have 0<ϑ≤10<\vartheta\leq 1. Our goal is to construct a random subset of PP with purchase probabilities exactly (ϑ​zi)i∈ℳ(\vartheta z_{i})_{i\in\mathcal{M}}.

For a retention vector β∈[0,1]M\beta\in[0,1]^{M}, independently retain each product i∈Pi\in P with probability βi\beta_{i}, using draws independent of PP. Denote the resulting assortment by Qβ⊆PQ^{\beta}\subseteq P, and write ξi​(β):=𝔼⁡[ϕi​(Qβ)]\xi_{i}(\beta):=\mathbb{E}[\phi_{i}(Q^{\beta})]. Its inclusion indicators are independent, with probabilities pi​βip_{i}\beta_{i}.

Each ξi\xi_{i} is continuous in β\beta, since it is a finite sum of purchase probabilities weighted by polynomials in the retention probabilities. Moreover, writing Q−iβ:=Qβ∖{i}Q^{\beta}_{-i}:=Q^{\beta}\setminus\{i\}, independence gives

ξi​(β)=pi​βi​𝔼​[ϕi​({i}∪Q−iβ)].\xi_{i}(\beta)=p_{i}\beta_{i}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\phi_{i}(\{i\}\cup Q^{\beta}_{-i})\right].

The expectation does not depend on βi\beta_{i}, so ξi\xi_{i} is linear and nondecreasing in its own coordinate. Under common random draws, increasing another coordinate βj\beta_{j} can only add a competing product; regularity therefore implies that it cannot increase ξi\xi_{i}.

The next lemma supplies the key boundary condition: if all other purchase probabilities do not exceed their targets, fully retaining product ii suffices to reach its target.

Lemma 2 (Purchase target at full retention)

Fix i∈I+i\in I^{+}. If βi=1\beta_{i}=1 and ξj​(β)≤ϑ​zj\xi_{j}(\beta)\leq\vartheta z_{j} for every j≠ij\neq i, then ξi​(β)≥ϑ​zi\xi_{i}(\beta)\geq\vartheta z_{i}.

Proof.

Proof. Write Q:=QβQ:=Q^{\beta} and Q−i:=Q∖{i}Q_{-i}:=Q\setminus\{i\}. Since βi=1\beta_{i}=1, product ii belongs to QQ with probability pip_{i}, independently of Q−iQ_{-i}. For j≠ij\neq i, define

bj+:=𝔼⁡[ϕj​({i}∪Q−i)],bj−:=𝔼⁡[ϕj​(Q−i)].b_{j}^{+}:=\mathbb{E}[\phi_{j}(\{i\}\cup Q_{-i})],\hskip 20.00003ptb_{j}^{-}:=\mathbb{E}[\phi_{j}(Q_{-i})].

Independence gives ξj​(β)=pi​bj++(1−pi)​bj−\xi_{j}(\beta)=p_{i}b_{j}^{+}+(1-p_{i})b_{j}^{-} for every j≠ij\neq i. Since regularity implies bj+≤bj−b_{j}^{+}\leq b_{j}^{-}, we obtain bj+≤ξj​(β)≤ϑ​zjb_{j}^{+}\leq\xi_{j}(\beta)\leq\vartheta z_{j}. Every realization of {i}∪Q−i\{i\}\cup Q_{-i} contains ii. The equality case of Proposition 4, followed by Lemma 1, therefore gives

ξi​(β)\displaystyle\xi_{i}(\beta) =pi​𝔼​[ϕi​({i}∪Q−i)]=pi​[ai−∑j≠ihj​i​bj+]\displaystyle=p_{i}\mathbb{E}[\phi_{i}(\{i\}\cup Q_{-i})]=p_{i}\left[a_{i}-\sum_{j\neq i}h_{ji}b_{j}^{+}\right]
≥pi​[ai−ϑ​∑j≠ihj​i​zj]≥pi​[ai−ϑ⁡(ai−zi)]\displaystyle\geq p_{i}\left[a_{i}-\vartheta\sum_{j\neq i}h_{ji}z_{j}\right]\geq p_{i}\bigl[a_{i}-\vartheta(a_{i}-z_{i})\bigr]
=ϑ​zi+ai​[pi−ϑ⁡{pi+ρi​(1−pi)}]≥ϑ​zi,\displaystyle=\vartheta z_{i}+a_{i}\bigl[p_{i}-\vartheta\{p_{i}+\rho_{i}(1-p_{i})\}\bigr]\geq\vartheta z_{i},

where the last inequality follows from the definition of ϑ\vartheta. ■\blacksquare ∎

We now attain all targets simultaneously. Among retention vectors that keep every purchase probability at most its target, choose one maximizing total retention. If a product remains below its target, the preceding lemma implies that its retention probability is less than one. We can then increase this probability slightly without violating any target constraint, contradicting maximality.

Lemma 3 (Simultaneous balanced attenuation)

There exists β⋆∈[0,1]M\beta^{\star}\in[0,1]^{M}, with βi⋆=0\beta_{i}^{\star}=0 for i∉I+i\notin I^{+}, such that

ξi​(β⋆)=ϑ​zi,i∈ℳ.\xi_{i}(\beta^{\star})=\vartheta z_{i},\hskip 20.00003pti\in\mathcal{M}.
Proof.

Proof. Consider

𝒟:={β∈[0,1]M:βi=0for ​i∉I+,ξi​(β)≤ϑ​zifor ​i∈ℳ}.\mathcal{D}:=\left\{\beta\in[0,1]^{M}:\begin{array}[]{ll}\beta_{i}=0&\text{for }i\notin I^{+},\\ \xi_{i}(\beta)\leq\vartheta z_{i}&\text{for }i\in\mathcal{M}\end{array}\right\}.

The zero vector belongs to 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and continuity of the functions ξi\xi_{i} makes 𝒟\mathcal{D} closed. It is therefore a nonempty compact subset of [0,1]M[0,1]^{M}. Choose β⋆∈𝒟\beta^{\star}\in\mathcal{D} maximizing ∑i∈I+βi\sum_{i\in I^{+}}\beta_{i}.

Suppose that ξi​(β⋆)<ϑ​zi\xi_{i}(\beta^{\star})<\vartheta z_{i} for some i∈I+i\in I^{+}. Lemma 2 implies βi⋆<1\beta_{i}^{\star}<1, since all other purchase probabilities satisfy their target bounds. By continuity, a sufficiently small increase in βi⋆\beta_{i}^{\star} preserves its own constraint. This change cannot increase any ξj\xi_{j} with j≠ij\neq i, so the resulting vector remains in 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Its total retention is strictly larger, contradicting the choice of β⋆\beta^{\star}.

Thus, every target on I+I^{+} is attained. For i∉I+i\notin I^{+}, the restriction βi⋆=0\beta_{i}^{\star}=0 gives ξi​(β⋆)=0=ϑ​zi\xi_{i}(\beta^{\star})=0=\vartheta z_{i}, completing the proof. ■\blacksquare ∎

The balanced assortment now gives the desired revenue comparison directly.

Proof.

Proof of Theorem 2. The zero-bound cases were addressed above. Otherwise, take β⋆\beta^{\star} from Lemma 3. For every realization of PP and the thinning draws, Qβ⋆⊆PQ^{\beta^{\star}}\subseteq P, so f⁡(P)≥R⁡(Qβ⋆)f(P)\geq R(Q^{\beta^{\star}}). Taking expectations gives 𝔼⁡[f⁡(P)]≥𝔼⁡[R⁡(Qβ⋆)]=∑i∈ℳri​ξi​(β⋆)=ϑ​∑i∈ℳri​zi.\mathbb{E}[f(P)]\geq\mathbb{E}[R(Q^{\beta^{\star}})]=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}r_{i}\xi_{i}(\beta^{\star})=\vartheta\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}r_{i}z_{i}. Substituting the definition of ϑ\vartheta proves (17). For the final assertion, whenever zi>0z_{i}>0,

pi≥ρi1+ρi⟺pi≥ρi(1−pi)⟺pipi+ρi​(1−pi)≥12.p_{i}\geq\frac{\rho_{i}}{1+\rho_{i}}\hskip 10.00002pt\Longleftrightarrow\hskip 10.00002ptp_{i}\geq\rho_{i}(1-p_{i})\hskip 10.00002pt\Longleftrightarrow\hskip 10.00002pt\frac{p_{i}}{p_{i}+\rho_{i}(1-p_{i})}\geq\frac{1}{2}.
