The thinning is solely a proof device. The policy optimizes directly over PP and does not need to compute β⋆\beta^{\star}.

4.2 Sharpness

The uniform factor 1/21/2 cannot be improved even under MNL choice with equal revenues and a deterministic benchmark assortment. This remains true when each candidate-inclusion probability equals its normalized benchmark target, pi=ρip_{i}=\rho_{i}.

Proposition 5 (Sharpness of the uniform Markov extraction bound)

For every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exist an MNL choice model, equal positive product revenues, and a deterministic benchmark assortment BB with W=∑iri​zi>0W=\sum_{i}r_{i}z_{i}>0 such that an independent candidate set PP with inclusion probabilities pi=ρi=zi/aip_{i}=\rho_{i}=z_{i}/a_{i} satisfies 𝔼⁡[f⁡(P)]/W≤1/2+ε.{\mathbb{E}[f(P)]}/{W}\leq{1}/{2}+\varepsilon.

5 Independent Proposals and Revenue Extraction

We now return to the consecutive-stay system. We first use the SBLP target flows to generate independent copy proposals and derive the probability that each product is visible (Subsection 5.1). We then apply Theorem 2 to bound the expected revenue from the visible products relative to the SBLP benchmark (Subsection 5.2). Finally, we specify the target updates that reproduce the SBLP interval flows (Subsection 5.3).

5.1 Proposal Generation from the Fluid Solution

We build on the virtual-state construction of Hu and Wu (2026), which uses interval-flow variables to generate independent copy proposals. In their choice-based model, each physical copy is a customer-facing alternative; in our model, several interchangeable copies may belong to the same product. Treating these copies as separate alternatives without adjusting the choice model can change product purchase probabilities. We therefore make a product eligible if any copy proposes, retaining copy identities for assignment and updates.

Fix a feasible copy-level SBLP solution. To generate proposals, we maintain a virtual free-slot state ℱ^t​i​c⊆𝒩\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{tic}\subseteq\mathcal{N} for each copy (i,c)(i,c). For now, suppose that these states are mutually independent across copies at the beginning of each period and satisfy

ℙ⁡([a,b]∼ℱ^t​i​c)=xt​i​c​([a,b]),[a,b]∈𝒬.\mathbb{P}\bigl([a,b]\sim\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{tic}\bigr)=x_{tic}([a,b]),\hskip 20.00003pt[a,b]\in\mathcal{Q}. (18)

We use these states to define the proposal rule. Subsection 5.3 constructs updates preserving these properties. Section 7 verifies them for the implemented policy.

Copy proposals. In period tt, a copy can propose only if its virtual state contains ItI_{t}. When this condition holds, there is a unique maximal free interval containing ItI_{t}, which determines the proposal probability. Suppose that [a,b][a,b] is the maximal free interval of ℱ^t​i​c\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{tic} containing ItI_{t}. Conditional on this event, copy (i,c)(i,c) proposes with probability

πt​i​c​([a,b]):=yt​i​c​([a,b])pt​at​i​xt​i​c​([a,b]).\pi_{tic}([a,b]):=\frac{y_{tic}([a,b])}{p_{t}a_{ti}x_{tic}([a,b])}. (19)

We define the ratio as zero when xt​i​c​([a,b])=0x_{tic}([a,b])=0, in which case (9) also gives yt​i​c​([a,b])=0y_{tic}([a,b])=0. We also set πt​i​c​([a,b])=0\pi_{tic}([a,b])=0 for intervals that do not contain ItI_{t}. If the virtual state cannot accommodate ItI_{t}, the copy does not propose. Constraint (9) ensures that 0≤πt​i​c​([a,b])≤10\leq\pi_{tic}([a,b])\leq 1.

We use random draws independent across copies and of the current virtual states. With one copy per product under MNL, (19) recovers the rule of Hu and Wu (2026). Here, at​ia_{ti} is the singleton purchase probability under general Markov choice. Normalization by pt​at​ip_{t}a_{ti} enables the updates in Subsection 5.3 to reproduce the SBLP interval flows yt​i​c​([a,b])y_{tic}([a,b]).

Proposal marginals and product visibility. Although a copy may have several maximal free intervals, at most one can contain ItI_{t}. The corresponding events are therefore mutually exclusive. Define the marginal proposal probability of copy (i,c)(i,c) and the total proposal mass of product ii by

ρt​i​c:=∑[a,b]∈𝒬xt​i​c​([a,b])​πt​i​c​([a,b])=1pt​at​i​∑[a,b]∈𝒬yt​i​c​([a,b])andρt​i:=∑c=1Ciρt​i​c.\displaystyle\rho_{tic}:=\sum_{[a,b]\in\mathcal{Q}}x_{tic}([a,b])\pi_{tic}([a,b])=\frac{1}{p_{t}a_{ti}}\sum_{[a,b]\in\mathcal{Q}}y_{tic}([a,b])\hskip 10.00002pt\textrm{and}\hskip 10.00002pt\rho_{ti}:=\sum_{c=1}^{C_{i}}\rho_{tic}. (20)

Thus, ρt​i​c\rho_{tic} is the probability that copy (i,c)(i,c) proposes, and ρt​i\rho_{ti} is the expected number of proposing copies of product ii.

We call product ii visible if at least one of its copies proposes, and write ρ~t​i\widetilde{\rho}_{ti} for its visibility probability. A visible product is eligible for the subsequent assortment decision and appears at most once in the offered assortment. Because several copies may propose simultaneously, ρ~t​i\widetilde{\rho}_{ti} need not equal the total proposal mass ρt​i\rho_{ti}. The following lemma connects these quantities to the SBLP sales targets.

Lemma 4 (Proposal marginals and visibility)

Suppose that, at the beginning of period tt, the virtual free-slot states are mutually independent across copies and satisfy the interval-marginal identities in (18). Under the proposal rule above, the following statements hold.

  1. (i)

    Sales targets and normalization. For every product ii and copy c∈[Ci]c\in[C_{i}],

    zt​i=at​i​ρt​i,0≤ρt​i​c≤ρt​i≤1.z_{ti}=a_{ti}\rho_{ti},\hskip 20.00003pt0\leq\rho_{tic}\leq\rho_{ti}\leq 1.
  2. (ii)

    Independent proposals and visibility. The copy-proposal indicators are mutually independent, with copy (i,c)(i,c) proposing with probability ρt​i​c\rho_{tic}. The visible-product indicators are also mutually independent across products, with

    ρ~t​i=1−∏c=1Ci(1−ρt​i​c).\widetilde{\rho}_{ti}=1-\prod_{c=1}^{C_{i}}(1-\rho_{tic}). (21)
  3. (iii)

    Capacity aggregation. For every product ii,

    ρ~t​i≥1−e−ρt​i≥ρt​i1+ρt​i≥ρt​i2.\widetilde{\rho}_{ti}\geq 1-e^{-\rho_{ti}}\geq\frac{\rho_{ti}}{1+\rho_{ti}}\geq\frac{\rho_{ti}}{2}.

Under the symmetric lift, all copies of product ii have the same marginal proposal probability, ρt​i​c=ρt​i/Ci\rho_{tic}=\rho_{ti}/C_{i}. Hence, (21) simplifies to

ρ~t​i=1−(1−ρt​iCi)Ci.\widetilde{\rho}_{ti}=1-\left(1-\frac{\rho_{ti}}{C_{i}}\right)^{C_{i}}.

With one copy per product, visibility equals the normalized sales target: ρ~t​i=ρt​i=zt​i/at​i\widetilde{\rho}_{ti}=\rho_{ti}=z_{ti}/a_{ti}. With multiple copies, the visibility probability can be strictly smaller than this target. Part (iii) verifies the condition for half-revenue extraction in Theorem 2, uniformly over product capacities.

5.2 Revenue Extraction from Independent Proposals

Our policy selects a revenue-maximizing assortment from the visible products. We compare the resulting expected revenue with the product-level SBLP benchmark by applying Theorem 2.

Benchmark and Visible-Set Revenue. Fix a period and suppress its time index. All revenues below are conditional on an arrival; the factor ptp_{t} is restored in the online performance analysis. Let BB have the SBLP assortment distribution θ\theta. In the notation of Section 4, its purchase probabilities are zi=𝔼⁡[ϕi​(B)]z_{i}=\mathbb{E}[\phi_{i}(B)], and zi=ai​ρiz_{i}=a_{i}\rho_{i} by Lemma 4. Its expected revenue W:=∑i∈ℳri​ziW:=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}r_{i}z_{i} is the period’s conditional SBLP benchmark. The policy does not sample BB.

The visible proposal set PvisP_{\rm vis} contains product ii if and only if at least one of its copies proposes. For a realization Pvis=AP_{\rm vis}=A, offering an optimal assortment yields expected revenue f⁡(A)f(A). Thus, 𝔼⁡[f⁡(Pvis)]\mathbb{E}[f(P_{\rm vis})] is the expected revenue from offering a revenue-maximizing assortment from the visible products, conditional on a customer arrival. The desired bound follows from nonnegativity when W=0W=0, so we assume W>0W>0.

Revenue Guarantee. By Lemma 4, products enter PvisP_{\rm vis} independently with probabilities ρ~i≥ρi/(1+ρi)\widetilde{\rho}_{i}\geq\rho_{i}/(1+\rho_{i}). Applying Theorem 2 with pi=ρ~ip_{i}=\widetilde{\rho}_{i} yields the following corollary.

Corollary 1 (Multi-capacity visible-set extraction)

The visible proposal set satisfies

𝔼[f(Pvis)]≥(mini:zi>0ρ~iρ~i+ρi​(1−ρ~i))∑i∈ℳrizi≥12∑i∈ℳrizi.\mathbb{E}[f(P_{\rm vis})]\geq\left(\min_{i:z_{i}>0}\frac{\widetilde{\rho}_{i}}{\widetilde{\rho}_{i}+\rho_{i}(1-\widetilde{\rho}_{i})}\right)\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}r_{i}z_{i}\geq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}r_{i}z_{i}.

The first bound retains the actual visibility probabilities and can give a guarantee strictly stronger than 1/21/2. The uniform 1/21/2 bound holds regardless of the number of copies or the allocation of proposal mass across them. Thus, aggregating multiple copy proposals into a single visible product introduces no additional factor depending on the product capacities.

5.3 Target Updates and Flow Realizability

We now construct virtual-state updates that preserve the interval marginals and independence assumed in Subsection 5.1. The update rule must ensure that the joint probability of [a,b][a,b] being present and ItI_{t} being removed from it equals the SBLP flow yt​i​c​([a,b])y_{tic}([a,b]). We first give a direct update rule, then show that it can be implemented through the proposal rule followed by a target update with probability pt​at​ip_{t}a_{ti}.

Lemma 5 (Realizability of copy-level interval flows)

Fix a feasible copy-level SBLP solution. For each copy (i,c)(i,c), initialize ℱ^1​i​c=𝒩\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{1ic}=\mathcal{N}. In period tt, if ItI_{t} is contained in a maximal free interval [a,b][a,b] of ℱ^t​i​c\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{tic}, remove ItI_{t} from the virtual state with conditional probability

κt​i​c​([a,b]):=yt​i​c​([a,b])xt​i​c​([a,b]),\kappa_{tic}([a,b]):=\frac{y_{tic}([a,b])}{x_{tic}([a,b])}, (22)

where the ratio is defined as zero when xt​i​c​([a,b])=0x_{tic}([a,b])=0. In all other cases, leave the state unchanged. Denote the resulting state by ℱ^t+1,i,c\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{t+1,i,c}. Then, for every copy (i,c)(i,c), period t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}, and interval [a,b]∈𝒬[a,b]\in\mathcal{Q},

ℙ⁡([a,b]∼ℱ^t​i​c)=xt​i​c​([a,b]).\mathbb{P}\bigl([a,b]\sim\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{tic}\bigr)=x_{tic}([a,b]). (23)

If the transition draws are independent across copies and periods, the virtual states are mutually independent across copies at the beginning of each period.

By (9) and pt​at​i≤1p_{t}a_{ti}\leq 1, the transition probability is well defined. If the current interval marginal equals xt​i​c​([a,b])x_{tic}([a,b]), the joint probability that [a,b][a,b] is present and cut is xt​i​c​([a,b])​κt​i​c​([a,b])=yt​i​c​([a,b])x_{tic}([a,b])\kappa_{tic}([a,b])=y_{tic}([a,b]). The persistence and residual-interval events therefore reproduce (10). Induction from the initial condition gives the prescribed marginals. Independent transition draws across copies preserve their independence.

Remark 1

To implement the transitions in Lemma 5 through proposals, we require the following target-update law: conditional on the current virtual states and realized proposals, the update indicators of all proposed copies are mutually independent, and each proposed copy of product ii is updated with probability pt​at​ip_{t}a_{ti}. Nonproposing copies remain unchanged. Conditional on the current virtual states and averaging over the proposal draws, the probability of removing ItI_{t} from its containing maximal free interval [a,b][a,b] is

πt​i​c​([a,b])​pt​at​i=yt​i​c​([a,b])xt​i​c​([a,b])=κt​i​c​([a,b]),\pi_{tic}([a,b])p_{t}a_{ti}=\frac{y_{tic}([a,b])}{x_{tic}([a,b])}=\kappa_{tic}([a,b]),

with the stated zero-denominator convention. Together with independent proposal draws, this update law reproduces the direct transitions jointly across copies.

It remains to couple these virtual updates with customer purchases so that every purchase can be assigned to an updated copy. Section 6 constructs such a coupling while preserving the prescribed joint update law.

6 Purchase–Update Coupling

We now couple customer purchases with the virtual updates specified in Remark 1. In each nonterminal period, conditional on the current virtual states and realized proposals, the prescribed update law selects each proposed copy of product ii independently with probability pt​at​ip_{t}a_{ti}. The coupling must recover this joint law after averaging over purchase outcomes, while ensuring that every purchase is assigned to an updated proposed copy of the purchased product. This construction reproduces the SBLP interval flows and, together with the containment of virtual availability within physical availability, ensures feasible assignment.

6.1 Purchase–Update Coupling Conditions

Fix a nonterminal period and suppress the time index. Condition on the current virtual states and realized copy proposals. Let mm denote the number of visible products, indexed by i∈[m]i\in[m]. For each product ii, let mi≥1m_{i}\geq 1 denote the number of its proposed copies, indexed locally by ℓ∈[mi]\ell\in[m_{i}]. Copies retain their physical identities for assignment, while each product appears at most once in the assortment. The static assortment oracle selects S∈arg​maxA⊆[m]⁡R​(A)S\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{A\subseteq[m]}R(A), where R⁡(A):=∑i∈Ari​ϕi​(A)R(A):=\sum_{i\in A}r_{i}\phi_{i}(A). All probabilities below are also conditional on SS.

The policy draws an independent gate G∼Bernoulli⁡(γ)G\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\gamma), with γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1], before observing the arrival outcome. An arriving customer is offered SS if G=1G=1 and the empty assortment otherwise. Subsection 7.1 specifies γ\gamma; setting γ=1\gamma=1 gives the ungated policy.

Let J∈{0,1,…,m}J\in\{0,1,\ldots,m\} denote the purchase outcome: J=iJ=i means that product ii is purchased, and J=0J=0 denotes no purchase due to no arrival, a closed gate, or selection of the outside option. The purchase probabilities are qi:=ℙ⁡(J=i)=γ​p​ϕi​(S)q_{i}:=\mathbb{P}(J=i)=\gamma p\phi_{i}(S) for i∈Si\in S, qi=0q_{i}=0 otherwise, and q0:=1−∑i=1mqiq_{0}:=1-\sum_{i=1}^{m}q_{i}, where pp is the arrival probability.

For each proposed copy ℓ∈[mi]\ell\in[m_{i}] of product ii, let Xi​ℓX_{i\ell} indicate whether it receives a virtual update. The target-update law in Remark 1 requires mutually independent indicators Xi​ℓ∼Bernoulli⁡(αi)X_{i\ell}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\alpha_{i}), where αi:=p​ai\alpha_{i}:=pa_{i} and ai:=ϕi​({i})a_{i}:=\phi_{i}(\{i\}). The gate changes the purchase probabilities but leaves this joint update law unchanged. Every purchase must be assigned to an updated proposed copy of the purchased product. Updates to other copies remove the requested interval only from their virtual free-slot sets, without reserving physical capacity.

Product-Level Coupling Conditions. Define Ui:=𝟏{∑ℓ=1miXi​ℓ≥1}U_{i}:=\mathbf{1}\{\sum_{\ell=1}^{m_{i}}X_{i\ell}\geq 1\} and U:={i∈[m]:Ui=1}U:=\{i\in[m]:U_{i}=1\}. Under the prescribed copy-update law, the UiU_{i} are independent Bernoulli indicators with parameters ηi:=1−(1−αi)mi\eta_{i}:=1-(1-\alpha_{i})^{m_{i}}.

We seek a coupling that preserves ℙ⁡(J=j)=qj\mathbb{P}(J=j)=q_{j} and ensures that every purchased product belongs to the update set:

J=i⟹i∈U,i∈[m],almost surely.J=i\hskip 10.00002pt\Longrightarrow\hskip 10.00002pti\in U,\hskip 20.00003pti\in[m],\hskip 10.00002pt\text{almost surely}. (24)

Averaging over the purchase outcome must recover the prescribed independent product-update law: for every u=(u1,…,um)∈{0,1}mu=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{m})\in\{0,1\}^{m},

∑j∈{0,…,m}qj>0qj​Pr⁡((U1,…,Um)=u∣J=j)=∏i=1mηiui​(1−ηi)1−ui.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in\{0,\ldots,m\}\\ q_{j}>0\end{subarray}}q_{j}\Pr\bigl((U_{1},\ldots,U_{m})=u\mid J=j\bigr)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\eta_{i}^{u_{i}}(1-\eta_{i})^{1-u_{i}}. (25)

The update indicators need not be independent conditional on JJ. In particular, observing J=iJ=i forces Ui=1U_{i}=1.

In the single-copy MNL setting, Hu and Wu (2026) generate virtual updates after observing the customer’s choice, ensuring that the copy fulfilling the purchase is updated and recovering the independent update law after averaging over outcomes. We extend this approach to multiple copies and general Markov chain choice by characterizing when the purchase and update distributions admit such a coupling.

For any A⊆[m]A\subseteq[m], (24) implies {J∈A}⊆{U∩A≠∅}\{J\in A\}\subseteq\{U\cap A\neq\varnothing\}, yielding the necessary inequalities below. The priority-rule representation in the next subsection establishes their sufficiency constructively.

Lemma 6 (Hall-type coupling characterization)

Let J∈{0,1,…,m}J\in\{0,1,\ldots,m\} have probabilities (q0,q1,…,qm)(q_{0},q_{1},\ldots,q_{m}), and let U⊆[m]U\subseteq[m] have mutually independent Bernoulli(ηi)(\eta_{i}) indicators. A coupling of JJ and UU satisfying (24) exists if and only if

∑i∈Aqi≤1−∏i∈A(1−ηi),A⊆[m].\sum_{i\in A}q_{i}\leq 1-\prod_{i\in A}(1-\eta_{i}),\hskip 20.00003ptA\subseteq[m]. (26)

The two sides of (26) are the probability of purchasing a product in AA and the probability that at least one product in AA receives an update, respectively. Regularity and mi≥1m_{i}\geq 1 give qi≤αi≤ηiq_{i}\leq\alpha_{i}\leq\eta_{i}, so the singleton conditions always hold. Larger subsets require additional conditions because purchase events are mutually exclusive, whereas update events can overlap.

For example, suppose p=γ=1p=\gamma=1, one copy of each of two products proposes, and both products are offered. The customer starts at either product with equal probability and transitions directly to the outside option if that product is unavailable. Then q1=q2=η1=η2=1/2q_{1}=q_{2}=\eta_{1}=\eta_{2}=1/2. Both singleton conditions hold, but the condition for A={1,2}A=\{1,2\} fails: a purchase occurs with probability one, whereas at least one update occurs with probability only 3/43/4. Hence, no coupling can support every purchase while preserving the independent update law.

The gate reduces purchase probabilities while preserving the update distribution. Subsection 7.1 shows that γ=1−1/e\gamma=1-1/e guarantees all subset inequalities uniformly over Markov chain choice models and proposal realizations. Under MNL, they hold with γ=1\gamma=1, so no gate is needed. Assuming (26) holds, we next construct a sampler conditional on the observed purchase outcome and lift its product-level updates to individual copies.

6.2 Priority-Rule Representation and Conditional Sampling

Lemma 6 characterizes when the desired coupling exists. To construct it, we first draw UU from its prescribed independent Bernoulli distribution and use a randomized priority rule to generate an auxiliary purchase outcome. We then reverse the sampling order to generate updates conditional on the actual purchase outcome.

Let π=(i1,…,ik)\pi=(i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}) be an ordered list of distinct products in [m][m], allowing k=0k=0. We examine the listed products in order and select the first one belonging to UU. If none belongs to UU, we return zero. We call this selection procedure a priority rule and define

𝗌𝖾𝗅π(U):={imin⁡{ℓ∈[k]:iℓ∈U},U∩{i1,…,ik}≠∅,0,otherwise.\mathsf{sel}_{\pi}(U):=\begin{cases}i_{\min\{\ell\in[k]:i_{\ell}\in U\}},&U\cap\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\}\neq\varnothing,\\[5.69054pt] 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

For every i∈[m]i\in[m], 𝗌𝖾𝗅π​(U)=i\mathsf{sel}_{\pi}(U)=i implies i∈Ui\in U, so each priority rule satisfies the purchase-support condition. The empty rule always returns zero.

A single priority rule need not produce the prescribed purchase probabilities. We therefore randomize over rules. The following proposition shows that, whenever the Hall-type conditions hold, a mixture of at most m+1m+1 priority rules reproduces the target purchase distribution exactly.

Proposition 6 (Priority-rule decomposition)

Suppose Ui∼Bernoulli⁡(ηi)U_{i}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\eta_{i}) independently for i∈[m]i\in[m]. For an ordered list π=(i1,…,ik)\pi=(i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}), define vπ=(v1π,…,vmπ)v^{\pi}=(v_{1}^{\pi},\ldots,v_{m}^{\pi}) by

viℓπ:=ℙ(𝗌𝖾𝗅π(U)=iℓ)=ηiℓ∏s<ℓ(1−ηis),ℓ=1,…,k,v^{\pi}_{i_{\ell}}:=\mathbb{P}\bigl(\mathsf{sel}_{\pi}(U)=i_{\ell}\bigr)=\eta_{i_{\ell}}\prod_{s<\ell}(1-\eta_{i_{s}}),\hskip 20.00003pt\ell=1,\ldots,k,

and set viπ:=0v_{i}^{\pi}:=0 for products omitted from π\pi. The no-selection probability is

v0π:=ℙ⁡(𝗌𝖾𝗅π​(U)=0)=∏ℓ=1k(1−ηiℓ)=1−∑i=1mviπ,v_{0}^{\pi}:=\mathbb{P}\bigl(\mathsf{sel}_{\pi}(U)=0\bigr)=\prod_{\ell=1}^{k}(1-\eta_{i_{\ell}})=1-\sum_{i=1}^{m}v_{i}^{\pi},

where an empty product equals one.

If q=(q1,…,qm)∈ℝ+mq=(q_{1},\ldots,q_{m})\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m} satisfies (26), then there exist priority rules π1,…,πL\pi^{1},\ldots,\pi^{L} and weights λ1,…,λL≥0\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{L}\geq 0, with L≤m+1L\leq m+1 and ∑h=1Lλh=1\sum_{h=1}^{L}\lambda_{h}=1, such that

q=∑h=1Lλh​vπh.q=\sum_{h=1}^{L}\lambda_{h}v^{\pi^{h}}. (27)

For rational qq and η\eta, such a decomposition can be computed in polynomial time using a greedy priority-rule oracle. The fixed irrational gate is handled by the rational reduction in Appendix D.3.

This representation follows from the classical greedy description of polymatroids (Edmonds 2003), applied to the coverage function g⁡(A)=1−∏i∈A(1−ηi)g(A)=1-\prod_{i\in A}(1-\eta_{i}). Appendix D.2 gives the proof and the decomposition algorithm.

Given this decomposition, construct the auxiliary joint distribution as follows. Draw the indicators UiU_{i} independently with probabilities ηi\eta_{i}. Independently of UU, draw H∈[L]H\in[L] with ℙ⁡(H=h)=λh\mathbb{P}(H=h)=\lambda_{h}, and set

Jf:=𝗌𝖾𝗅πH​(U).J^{\rm f}:=\mathsf{sel}_{\pi^{H}}(U).

Conditional on H=hH=h, the outcome probabilities are (v0πh,v1πh,…,vmπh)(v_{0}^{\pi^{h}},v_{1}^{\pi^{h}},\ldots,v_{m}^{\pi^{h}}). The decomposition and normalization therefore give

ℙ(Jf=j)=∑h=1Lλhvjπh=qj,j=0,1,…,m.\mathbb{P}(J^{\rm f}=j)=\sum_{h=1}^{L}\lambda_{h}v_{j}^{\pi^{h}}=q_{j},\hskip 20.00003ptj=0,1,\ldots,m.

The update indicators retain their prescribed independent Bernoulli distribution, and every priority rule ensures that Jf=iJ^{\rm f}=i implies i∈Ui\in U. Thus, (Jf,U)(J^{\rm f},U) has both required marginal distributions and satisfies the purchase-support condition.

Conditional Sampling After the Customer Outcome. The auxiliary outcome JfJ^{\rm f} defines the joint law; the online policy observes the actual purchase outcome JJ and then samples from ℒ⁡(H,U∣Jf=j)\mathcal{L}(H,U\mid J^{\rm f}=j) when J=jJ=j. For an observed outcome J=jJ=j with qj>0q_{j}>0, Bayes’ rule gives

ℙ⁡(H=h∣Jf=j)=λh​vjπhqj,h∈[L].\mathbb{P}(H=h\mid J^{\rm f}=j)=\frac{\lambda_{h}v_{j}^{\pi^{h}}}{q_{j}},\hskip 20.00003pth\in[L].

After drawing HH, the policy conditions the update indicators on the selected rule returning jj. If j=i>0j=i>0, it sets Ui=1U_{i}=1 and the indicators of products preceding ii in the rule to zero. If j=0j=0, it sets all indicators listed in the rule to zero. In either case, the remaining indicators are sampled independently with their original Bernoulli parameters. Thus, products omitted from the rule may receive updates even when no purchase occurs.

Because JJ and JfJ^{\rm f} have the same distribution, this conditional sampling reproduces the auxiliary joint law after averaging over JJ. Algorithm 3 in Appendix D.4 gives the detailed procedure.

Proposition 7 (Correctness of the posterior sampler)

Suppose (26) holds and JJ has probabilities (q0,q1,…,qm)(q_{0},q_{1},\ldots,q_{m}). Given a decomposition satisfying (27), Algorithm 3 has the following properties:

  1. (i)

    For every i∈[m]i\in[m], J=iJ=i implies i∈Ui\in U almost surely.

  2. (ii)

    After averaging over JJ, the indicators (Ui)i∈[m](U_{i})_{i\in[m]} are mutually independent Bernoulli(ηi)(\eta_{i}) variables. Equivalently, their distribution satisfies (25).

Given a priority decomposition of size LL as in Proposition 6, the posterior weights for all positive-probability outcomes can be precomputed in O⁡((m+1)​L)O((m+1)L) arithmetic operations. Each execution uses O⁡(m+L)O(m+L) arithmetic operations, one categorical draw, and at most mm Bernoulli draws. Since L≤m+1L\leq m+1, preprocessing requires O⁡(m2)O(m^{2}) arithmetic operations and each execution requires O⁡(m)O(m) arithmetic operations and random draws.

6.3 Copy-Level Updates and Physical Assignment

The product-level sampler determines whether each product has at least one proposed copy selected for a virtual update. We now select the individual copies consistently with these outcomes. Given UU, generate each product’s update vector using its own indicator UiU_{i} and independent random draws across products:

  • •

    If Ui=0U_{i}=0, set Xi​ℓ=0X_{i\ell}=0 for every ℓ∈[mi]\ell\in[m_{i}].

  • •

    If Ui=1U_{i}=1, sample (Xi​1,…,Xi​mi)(X_{i1},\ldots,X_{im_{i}}) from the joint law of mim_{i} independent Bernoulli(αi)(\alpha_{i}) variables, conditional on at least one success. Thus, for every nonzero vector x∈{0,1}mix\in\{0,1\}^{m_{i}},

    ℙ⁡((Xi​1,…,Xi​mi)=x∣Ui=1)=αi∥x∥1​(1−αi)mi−∥x∥1ηi,\mathbb{P}\bigl((X_{i1},\ldots,X_{im_{i}})=x\mid U_{i}=1\bigr)=\frac{\alpha_{i}^{\lVert x\rVert_{1}}(1-\alpha_{i})^{m_{i}-\lVert x\rVert_{1}}}{\eta_{i}}, (28)

    where ηi=1−(1−αi)mi\eta_{i}=1-(1-\alpha_{i})^{m_{i}}.

If ηi=0\eta_{i}=0, then Ui=0U_{i}=0 almost surely, so the conditional law in (28) is never used.

After averaging over JJ, the product indicators UiU_{i} have their prescribed independent distribution. For each product, mixing the zero-update and nonempty-update branches recovers the joint law of independent Bernoulli(αi)(\alpha_{i}) copy updates. Because the lifting uses independent random draws across products, the resulting updates are independent across all proposed copies. Appendix E.4 gives the proof and a direct sampler requiring O⁡(mi)O(m_{i}) operations per product.

If J=iJ=i, Proposition 7 ensures Ui=1U_{i}=1, so at least one proposed copy of product ii is selected for an update. Assign the purchase to one such copy and reserve the requested interval on it. Regardless of the purchase outcome, remove the requested interval from the virtual free-slot set of every proposed copy selected for an update, across all products. Only the assigned copy receives a physical reservation; all other updates are virtual discards. When J=0J=0, every update is a virtual discard.

Thus, whenever (26) holds, the construction preserves the independent copy-update law and assigns every purchase to an updated proposed copy. Subsection 7.1 selects a gate that guarantees these conditions.

7 Online Policy and Performance Guarantees

We now combine the proposal mechanism and purchase–update coupling into an online policy. We first choose the gate probability to ensure that the coupling conditions hold for every proposal realization. We then describe the policy and establish its feasibility and approximation guarantees.

7.1 Gate Selection

The coupling constructed in Section 6 requires the Hall-type inequalities in Lemma 6. We now choose the gate probability so that these inequalities hold for every proposal realization, while preserving the prescribed independent copy-update law.

Fix a nonterminal period and suppress the time index. Treat the current virtual states, realized copy proposals, and preselected assortment SS as fixed. For each visible product ii, let mi≥1m_{i}\geq 1 denote the number of its proposed copies. Each proposed copy must receive a virtual update with probability p​aipa_{i}, where ai:=ϕi​({i})a_{i}:=\phi_{i}(\{i\}), independently of the other proposed copies. Thus, product ii receives at least one update with probability ηi:=1−(1−p​ai)mi\eta_{i}:=1-(1-pa_{i})^{m_{i}}.

Recall that the policy draws an independent gate G∼Bernoulli⁡(γ)G\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\gamma) before observing the arrival outcome and offers SS if the gate is open and the customer arrives. A closed gate results in an empty offered assortment. The resulting purchase probabilities are qi=γ​p​ϕi​(S)q_{i}=\gamma p\phi_{i}(S) for i∈Si\in S and zero for visible products outside SS. The coupling must recover the prescribed independent copy-update law after averaging over the gate, arrival, and choice outcomes summarized by JJ.

By Lemma 6, the gate is feasible if and only if

γ​p​∑i∈Aϕi​(S)≤1−∏i∈A(1−ηi),A⊆S.\gamma p\sum_{i\in A}\phi_{i}(S)\leq 1-\prod_{i\in A}(1-\eta_{i}),\hskip 20.00003ptA\subseteq S. (29)

It suffices to consider subsets of SS: products outside SS have zero purchase probability, and adding them to a subset can only increase its probability of receiving at least one update. Because the gate is independent of arrival and choice, the expected revenue conditional on an arrival is γ​R​(S)\gamma R(S).

For every visible product, mi≥1m_{i}\geq 1 implies ηi=1−(1−p​ai)mi≥p​ai\eta_{i}=1-(1-pa_{i})^{m_{i}}\geq pa_{i}. Thus, for any A⊆SA\subseteq S, 1−∏i∈A(1−ηi)≥1−∏i∈A(1−p​ai).1-\prod_{i\in A}(1-\eta_{i})\geq 1-\prod_{i\in A}(1-pa_{i}). The right-hand side is the update probability when each product in AA has exactly one proposed copy. A gate that satisfies all Hall-type inequalities in this case therefore remains feasible with any larger number of proposed copies.

Definition 1 (Product-update compatibility)

For a fixed choice model ϕ\phi, define

Γ⁡(ϕ):=min⁡{1,infp∈(0,1],S⊆ℳ,A⊆S,∑i∈Aϕi​(S)>01−∏i∈A(1−p​ai)p​∑i∈Aϕi​(S)}.\Gamma(\phi):=\min\left\{1,\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}p\in(0,1],\ S\subseteq\mathcal{M},\ A\subseteq S,\sum_{i\in A}\phi_{i}(S)>0\end{subarray}}\frac{1-\prod_{i\in A}(1-pa_{i})}{p\sum_{i\in A}\phi_{i}(S)}\right\}. (30)

Each ratio in (30) compares the probability of at least one update in AA, with one proposed copy per product, to the ungated purchase probability of AA. Thus, Γ⁡(ϕ)\Gamma(\phi) is the largest gate acceptance probability that satisfies all these one-copy inequalities, uniformly over pp, SS, and AA. Every γ∈[0,Γ⁡(ϕ)]\gamma\in[0,\Gamma(\phi)] consequently satisfies (29) for every proposal realization.

The following result gives a fixed gate that is valid for every Markov chain choice model.

Proposition 8 (Universal Markov coupling gate)

For every Markov chain choice model,

Γ⁡(ϕ)≥1−1e.\Gamma(\phi)\geq 1-\frac{1}{e}. (31)

Consequently, the fixed gate γ=1−1/e\gamma=1-1/e satisfies the Hall-type conditions in Lemma 6 for every proposal realization and every assortment selected from the visible products.

Proof.

Proof. Fix p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1], S⊆ℳS\subseteq\mathcal{M}, and A⊆SA\subseteq S, and set x:=p​∑i∈Aaix:=p\sum_{i\in A}a_{i}. Regularity gives ϕi​(S)≤ai\phi_{i}(S)\leq a_{i}, while the total purchase probability conditional on an arrival is at most one. Hence, p​∑i∈Aϕi​(S)≤min⁡{p,x}≤min⁡{1,x}.p\sum_{i\in A}\phi_{i}(S)\leq\min\{p,x\}\leq\min\{1,x\}. Using 1−y≤e−y1-y\leq e^{-y}, we obtain

1−∏i∈A(1−p​ai)≥1−e−x≥(1−1e)​min⁡{1,x}≥(1−1e)​p​∑i∈Aϕi​(S).\displaystyle 1-\prod_{i\in A}(1-pa_{i})\geq 1-e^{-x}\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)\min\{1,x\}\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)p\sum_{i\in A}\phi_{i}(S).

The second inequality follows from the concavity of 1−e−x1-e^{-x} on [0,1][0,1] and its monotonicity for x≥1x\geq 1. Every ratio in (30) is therefore at least 1−1/e1-1/e, proving (31). Additional proposed copies only increase the probability of at least one update, so the same gate remains feasible. ■\blacksquare ∎

This proof uses only regularity and the fact that total purchase probability is at most one. The gate bound therefore applies to any regular discrete-choice model.

Sharpness of the uniform gate. The constant 1−1/e1-1/e in Proposition 8 is the largest scalar gate that works uniformly over all Markov chain choice models.

Proposition 9 (Sharpness of the universal Markov gate)

No scalar gate γ>1−1/e\gamma>1-1/e satisfies the required Hall-type inequalities uniformly over all Markov chain choice models. Hence, the constant 1−1/e1-1/e in Proposition 8 is best possible among uniform scalar gates.

This result concerns gates that must be valid throughout the Markov family. Gates tailored to the realized instance or different proposal and update mechanisms may permit stronger guarantees.

Lossless coupling under MNL. Under the positive-outside normalization in (2), MNL is a special case of Markov chain choice. Its choice probabilities satisfy a stronger compatibility property: all Hall-type inequalities hold without gating. Consequently, the coupling can be implemented with γ=1\gamma=1.

Proposition 10 (Lossless product-update coupling under MNL)

Under the positive-outside normalization in (2), Γ⁡(ϕ)=1\Gamma(\phi)=1. Thus, the customer outcome can be coupled with the prescribed independent product-update law without attenuating the purchase probabilities.

These results specify the gate probabilities used below: γ=1−1/e\gamma=1-1/e under general Markov chain choice and γ=1\gamma=1 under MNL. We now combine these gates with the proposal and coupling constructions.

7.2 Online Policy

The policy uses an optimal SBLP solution to generate candidate products in each period. It first draws independent proposals from virtually feasible copies and makes a product visible whenever one of its copies proposes. It then selects a revenue-maximizing assortment from the visible products. In each nonterminal period, the policy applies the selected gate and, after observing the purchase outcome, samples virtual updates and assigns any purchase to an updated proposed copy of the purchased product. Together, the updates associated with purchases and virtual discards reproduce the SBLP interval flows used to generate future proposals.

Physical and virtual availability. For each copy (i,c)(i,c), the policy maintains an actual free-slot set ℱt​i​c\mathcal{F}_{tic} and a virtual free-slot set ℱ¯t​i​c\overline{\mathcal{F}}_{tic}, both initialized to 𝒩\mathcal{N}. The actual set changes only when a purchase is assigned to that copy; the virtual set determines its proposals. Removing an interval only from the virtual set is called a virtual discard. The policy maintains ℱ¯t​i​c⊆ℱt​i​c\overline{\mathcal{F}}_{tic}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{tic}, so every proposed copy can physically fulfill the request. In nonterminal periods, the updates of ℱ¯t​i​c\overline{\mathcal{F}}_{tic} implement the transitions defined for ℱ^t​i​c\widehat{\mathcal{F}}_{tic} in Lemma 5.

For example, in a nonterminal period, suppose two copies of a product propose and both receive virtual updates. If a purchase is assigned to the first copy, ItI_{t} is removed from both virtual sets but only from the first copy’s actual set. The second copy remains physically available for ItI_{t}; its update is a virtual discard.

Decisions and updates. Let 𝒪t​(A)\mathcal{O}_{t}(A) return a revenue-maximizing assortment contained in AA. We use γ=1−1/e\gamma=1-1/e under general Markov chain choice and γ=1\gamma=1 under MNL, as justified by Propositions 8 and 10, respectively. Remark 3 covers the MNL boundary case.

For each nonterminal period, we use the purchase–update coupling developed above as a subroutine. Given the proposals and selected assortment, it forms the purchase and update probabilities from Subsection 6.1 and computes the priority decomposition in Proposition 6. It then applies Algorithm 3 conditional on the observed purchase outcome and lifts the product updates to individual copies using Subsection 6.3. Appendix D.3 handles the fixed irrational gate.

Let Wt​iW_{ti} denote the labels of proposed copies of product ii selected for a virtual update. The coupling ensures Wt​i≠∅W_{ti}\neq\varnothing whenever Jt=iJ_{t}=i, allowing the purchase to be assigned to an updated copy. Updates are sampled even when Jt=0J_{t}=0; in that case, all updates are virtual discards.

The terminal period requires no gate or coupling because no further proposal distributions need to be preserved. Any purchase is assigned directly to a proposed copy, and the requested interval is removed from both of that copy’s states. Let PtP_{t} denote the set of products with at least one proposed copy in period tt. When Pt=∅P_{t}=\varnothing, the offered assortment and all update sets are empty.

In the terminal period, one could instead optimize over all physically available products 𝒜T\mathcal{A}_{T} and assign any purchase to a feasible copy. Since PT⊆𝒜TP_{T}\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{T}, we have fT​(𝒜T)≥fT​(PT)f_{T}(\mathcal{A}_{T})\geq f_{T}(P_{T}), so this modification weakly increases revenue and preserves the approximation guarantees. Algorithm 1 retains proposal-based assortment selection in every period for a uniform policy definition.

MNL assortment oracles. The required assortment oracles are efficient under MNL. For nonnegative product weights, an optimal assortment can be chosen as a prefix of the products ordered by nonincreasing weight (Talluri and van Ryzin 2004, Gallego et al. 2004). Sorting the products and evaluating the prefixes using cumulative sums requires O⁡(|A|​log⁡|A|)O(|A|\log|A|) arithmetic and comparison operations for a candidate set AA. This implements both the weighted assortment oracle used by the SBLP and the revenue-maximizing oracle used by the online policy.

7.3 State Invariants and Physical Feasibility

We first verify that the coupling produces the prescribed independent copy updates. We then use this update law to establish the virtual-state invariants and physical feasibility.

Lemma 7 (Exact copy-level update law)

Fix a nonterminal period t<Tt<T, and condition on the current virtual states, realized copy proposals, and preselected assortment S^t\widehat{S}_{t}. After averaging over JtJ_{t}, the update indicators of all proposed copies are mutually independent. Each proposed copy of product ii receives a virtual update with probability αt​i=pt​at​i\alpha_{ti}=p_{t}a_{ti}.

Lemma 7 follows from Proposition 7 and the copy-level lifting in Subsection 6.3, which together recover the prescribed joint update law.

Theorem 3 (Multi-capacity implementation invariants)

Algorithm 1 satisfies the following properties:

  1. (i)

    For every copy (i,c)(i,c) and t=1,…,T+1t=1,\ldots,T+1, ℱ¯t​i​c⊆ℱt​i​c\overline{\mathcal{F}}_{tic}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{tic} along every sample path.

  2. (ii)

    Every purchase is assigned to a physically feasible copy of the purchased product, and the requested interval is reserved on exactly one physical copy.

  3. (iii)

    At the beginning of every period t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}, ℙ⁡([a,b]∼ℱ¯t​i​c)=xt​i​c​([a,b])\mathbb{P}\bigl([a,b]\sim\overline{\mathcal{F}}_{tic}\bigr)=x_{tic}([a,b]) for every copy (i,c)(i,c) and interval [a,b]∈𝒬[a,b]\in\mathcal{Q}.

  4. (iv)

    At the beginning of every period t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}, the virtual free-slot sets are mutually independent across copies.

Consequently, actual occupancy never exceeds physical capacity.

The argument proceeds by induction over periods. Initially, all actual and virtual copies are fully available, so properties (i), (iii), and (iv) hold by the initialization and (11).

Virtual-state evolution. Consider a nonterminal period t<Tt<T and a virtually feasible copy whose maximal free interval [a,b][a,b] contains ItI_{t}. Conditional on the current virtual states, its probability of proposing and receiving an update is

πt​i​c​([a,b])​pt​at​i=yt​i​c​([a,b])xt​i​c​([a,b]),\pi_{tic}([a,b])p_{t}a_{ti}=\frac{y_{tic}([a,b])}{x_{tic}([a,b])},

where the ratio is defined as zero when its denominator is zero. This is the transition probability in Lemma 5. The proposal draws are independent across copies, and Lemma 7 gives independent updates conditional on the realized proposals. Since each proposed copy’s update probability pt​at​ip_{t}a_{ti} does not depend on which other copies propose, the joint transition law factors across copies and each copy’s transition depends only on its own virtual state. The virtual states therefore retain the prescribed interval marginals and independence through the beginning of period TT.

Physical feasibility. Suppose virtual containment holds at the beginning of period tt. A copy proposes only if its virtual state contains ItI_{t}, so every proposed copy is physically feasible. In a nonterminal period, the coupling assigns every purchase to an updated proposed copy. The policy removes ItI_{t} from both states of the assigned copy and only from the virtual states of other updated copies, preserving virtual containment. If no purchase occurs, actual states remain unchanged and virtual states can only shrink. In the terminal period, a purchase is assigned directly to a proposed copy and ItI_{t} is removed from both its states. Thus, every purchase reserves the requested interval on exactly one physically feasible copy, and containment holds through period boundary T+1T+1.

The distributional statements in (iii) and (iv) average over past outcomes; they do not condition on a realized purchase history.

7.4 Approximation Guarantees

We prove both parts of Theorem 1 using a common argument. Fix the optimal SBLP solution (x,y,z)(x,y,z) used by Algorithm 1. By Theorem 3, the virtual states at the beginning of each period have the prescribed interval marginals and are independent across copies. Corollary 1 therefore gives 𝔼⁡[ft​(Pt)]≥12​∑i∈ℳrt​i​zt​i\mathbb{E}[f_{t}(P_{t})]\geq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}r_{ti}z_{ti} for every period tt, where the expectation averages over the virtual states and proposals. The current arrival is independent of the candidate set. In each nonterminal period, the gate retains a fraction γ\gamma of the expected assortment revenue, and the coupling preserves the resulting purchase probabilities. The terminal period uses no gate. Consequently,

Vπ​(I)=γ​∑t=1T−1pt​𝔼​[ft​(Pt)]+pT​𝔼​[fT​(PT)]≥γ2​∑t=1Tpt​∑i∈ℳrt​i​zt​i=γ2​SBLPMCC⁡(I).\displaystyle V^{\pi}(I)=\gamma\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}p_{t}\mathbb{E}[f_{t}(P_{t})]+p_{T}\mathbb{E}[f_{T}(P_{T})]\geq\frac{\gamma}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}p_{t}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}r_{ti}z_{ti}=\frac{\gamma}{2}\operatorname{SBLP}_{\rm MC}^{C}(I).

The inequality follows from Corollary 1, γ≤1\gamma\leq 1, and nonnegative revenues. The final equality follows from optimality of the SBLP solution. Proposition 8 permits γ=1−1/e\gamma=1-1/e under general Markov chain choice, while Proposition 10 permits γ=1\gamma=1 under MNL. Substituting these values and applying the SBLP upper bound on Von​(I)V^{\rm on}(I) proves (3) and (4).

The following result shows that the 1/21/2 guarantee is tight for the proposed MNL policy relative to the optimal online benchmark.

Proposition 11 (Tightness for the proposed MNL policy)

There exists a sequence of one-period, unit-capacity MNL instances (Im)m≥1(I_{m})_{m\geq 1} such that

VπMNL​(Im)Von​(Im)⟶12.\frac{V^{\pi_{\rm MNL}}(I_{m})}{V^{\rm on}(I_{m})}\longrightarrow\frac{1}{2}. (32)

Hence, the 1/21/2 guarantee in Theorem 1(ii) is tight for the proposed MNL policy.

This tightness result concerns Algorithm 1, which uses independent proposals even in the terminal period. In a one-period instance, the optimal online policy offers a revenue-maximizing assortment from all available products, while the proposed policy first restricts the candidate set through independent proposals. The limiting loss therefore arises from this proposal step. The terminal-period modification described above is optimal on these one-period instances and is not covered by this tightness result.

Running time. The aggregate SBLP is solved once before the booking horizon, as established in Proposition 3. It contains O⁡(T​M​N2)O(TMN^{2}) interval variables, and forming the symmetric copy-level interval targets requires O⁡(T​N2​Ctot)O(TN^{2}C_{\mathrm{tot}}) arithmetic operations.

In each period, the policy solves an assortment problem over the realized visible set PtP_{t}. This problem is polynomial-time solvable under Markov chain choice and requires O⁡(m​log⁡(2+m))O(m\log(2+m)) arithmetic and comparison operations under MNL, where m:=|Pt|m:=|P_{t}|. In each nonterminal period, the policy also computes a priority decomposition for the induced purchase and update probabilities, using Proposition 6 and Appendix D.3. Given this decomposition, for m≥1m\geq 1, computing all posterior weights takes O⁡(m2)O(m^{2}) arithmetic operations, and one execution of the conditional sampler takes O⁡(m)O(m) operations. The copy-level sampling then takes O⁡(∑i∈Ptmt​i)O(\sum_{i\in P_{t}}m_{ti}) operations. These sampling counts treat random draws as primitives and exclude the polynomial-time computation of the decomposition. The assortment oracle and, in nonterminal periods, the priority decomposition are the main online optimization tasks.

The remaining state-maintenance operations are polynomial in the model dimensions. Under the computational convention stated at the beginning of the electronic companion, the bound Ctot≤M​TC_{\mathrm{tot}}\leq MT and the exact-sampling construction in Appendix D.3 imply that the complete policy has expected running time polynomial in T,N,MT,N,M and the model input size.

Remark 2

When Ci=1C_{i}=1 for every product, product visibility coincides with the unique copy’s proposal, whose marginal probability is ρt​i=zt​i/at​i\rho_{ti}=z_{ti}/a_{ti}. In each nonterminal period, conditional on the current virtual states and realized proposals, the prescribed update probability of a proposing copy is pt​at​ip_{t}a_{ti}. This specialization retains the resource-level proposal-discarding framework of Hu and Wu (2026), without any copy aggregation. Since the MNL coupling requires no gate, the improvement from 0.2710.271 to 1/21/2 follows from the stronger static revenue-extraction analysis.

Remark 3 (Zero outside-option attractiveness)

If the outside option has zero attractiveness in every period, the same ungated MNL policy satisfies the stronger guarantee

VπMNL​(I)≥(1−1e)​SBLPMCC⁡(I)≥(1−1e)​Von​(I).V^{\pi_{\rm MNL}}(I)\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)\operatorname{SBLP}_{\rm MC}^{C}(I)\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)V^{\rm on}(I).

In this case, at​i=1a_{ti}=1, and a highest-revenue singleton is optimal within any nonempty candidate set. Since the independent copy-proposal probabilities satisfy ∑cρt​i​c=zt​i\sum_{c}\rho_{tic}=z_{ti} and ∑izt​i≤1\sum_{i}z_{ti}\leq 1, a direct bound on the probability of seeing a product above each revenue threshold gives 𝔼⁡[ft​(Pt)]≥(1−1/e)​∑irt​i​zt​i\mathbb{E}[f_{t}(P_{t})]\geq(1-1/e)\sum_{i}r_{ti}z_{ti}. The Hall-type inequalities remain valid with γ=1\gamma=1, so the coupling introduces no further loss. Our policy attains the same 1−1/e1-1/e guarantee as Hu and Wu (2026) when the outside option has zero attractiveness in every period. Appendix E.8 establishes this guarantee for arbitrary copy multiplicities and shows that the factor is tight for the policy using the symmetric lift.

8 Conclusion

We study online assortment optimization under Markov chain choice when each booking reserves consecutive service slots on a single physical copy and each product may have multiple interchangeable copies. We formulate a copy-expanded SBLP and show that aggregating copies of the same product preserves its optimal value. The resulting target flows guide a proposal-discarding policy that includes each product at most once in each offered assortment while retaining copy identities for assignment. By keeping each virtual free-slot set within its actual counterpart, the policy ensures that every purchase is assigned to a copy available throughout the requested interval.

Our analysis separates static revenue extraction from dynamic implementation. A Markov-path argument shows that optimizing over products made available by independent copy proposals recovers at least half of the SBLP revenue benchmark in expectation. A coverage-polymatroid coupling then coordinates customer purchases with the prescribed independent virtual updates. A uniform gate with acceptance probability 1−1/e1-1/e ensures the feasibility of this coupling under general Markov choice, whereas MNL requires no gating. Together, these results yield approximation guarantees of (1−1/e)/2(1-1/e)/2 and 1/21/2, respectively, relative to the optimal nonanticipative online value, for arbitrary product capacities. Under MNL with zero outside-option attractiveness in every period, the guarantee improves to 1−1/e1-1/e.

The 1/21/2 extraction factor and the 1−1/e1-1/e uniform scalar-gate factor are separately sharp, and neither loss is an artifact of copy aggregation. These sharpness results do not establish tightness of the combined Markov guarantee, since the two worst cases need not coincide. Under MNL, the 1/21/2 guarantee is tight for the proposed policy even with one copy per product, but this policy-specific result does not rule out stronger guarantees for other policies. Further improvements may come from adapting the gate to the realized proposals or jointly redesigning proposal generation and virtual updates.

Proof.

Step 1: Define the assortment and purchase variables. Fix a feasible nonanticipative policy π\pi. Let ℋt\mathscr{H}_{t} be the information sigma-field immediately before the period-tt arrival, including the observed history and the policy randomization used to select the assortment. Let AtA_{t} denote the arrival indicator, and let JtJ_{t} denote the purchased product, with Jt=0J_{t}=0 when no arrival or no purchase occurs. By the arrival and choice assumptions, ℙπ​(At=1∣ℋt)=pt\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(A_{t}=1\mid\mathscr{H}_{t})=p_{t} and ℙπ​(At=1,Jt=i∣ℋt)=pt​ϕt​i​(St)\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(A_{t}=1,J_{t}=i\mid\mathscr{H}_{t})=p_{t}\phi_{ti}(S_{t}). Consequently, ∑S⊆ℳθt​S=1\sum_{S\subseteq\mathcal{M}}\theta_{tS}=1 and zt​i=∑S⊆ℳθt​S​ϕt​i​(S)z_{ti}=\sum_{S\subseteq\mathcal{M}}\theta_{tS}\phi_{ti}(S). Using the convention ϕt​i​(S)=0\phi_{ti}(S)=0 for i∉Si\notin S, these identities establish (6)–(7).

Let Dt​i​c​(K)D_{tic}(K) indicate that the period-tt customer arrives, purchases product ii, and is assigned to copy (i,c)(i,c), with KK as the maximal free interval containing the requested interval. These residuals are maximal free intervals. Their inner endpoints are adjacent to newly reserved slots, while their outer endpoints inherit maximality from the parent. Removing service slots cannot merge free intervals or alter any other maximal free interval.

For a fixed interval [a,b][a,b], persistence and creation as a residual are mutually exclusive. Although a reservation may create two different residuals, it cannot create the same interval twice. Symmetric lifting. Conversely, let (X,Y,θ,z)(X,Y,\theta,z) be a feasible aggregate solution. For every c∈[Ci]c\in[C_{i}], define xt​i​c​(K):=Xt​i​(K)/Cix_{tic}(K):=X_{ti}(K)/C_{i} and yt​i​c​(K):=Yt​i​(K)/Ciy_{tic}(K):=Y_{ti}(K)/C_{i}, again leaving θ\theta and zz unchanged. Dividing each aggregate interval-capacity constraint and balance equation by CiC_{i} gives the corresponding copy-level constraint. The aggregate initial condition likewise gives x1​i​c(K)=𝟏{K=[1,N]}x_{1ic}(K)=\mathbf{1}\{K=[1,N]\}. The two formulations consequently have the same attainable objective values and hence the same optimal value.

Proof.

Step 2: Construct a separation oracle for the dual. Consider a candidate dual solution. Its explicit constraints can be checked directly. For a fixed period tt, define di:=pt​βt​id_{i}:=p_{t}\beta_{ti}. Hence, an optimal assortment can be chosen within A+A^{+}. If A+=∅A^{+}=\varnothing, the empty assortment is optimal with value zero. Otherwise, separation reduces to (16) with nonnegative rewards.

We now give an exact implementation of this weighted assortment oracle. Suppress the period index, let A⊆ℳA\subseteq\mathcal{M} be the eligible products, and let wi≥0w_{i}\geq 0 be their rewards. Consider the stopping problem in which the chain may stop at a product i∈Ai\in A for reward wiw_{i}, must continue at products outside AA, and receives zero upon reaching the outside option. Its value is characterized by

s.t.\displaystyle\textnormal{s.t.} vj≥∑k∈ℳqj​k​vk,\displaystyle v_{j}\geq\sum_{k\in\mathcal{M}}q_{jk}v_{k}, j∈ℳ,\displaystyle j\in\mathcal{M},

The inequalities require vjv_{j} to dominate the value of continuation and, at eligible products, the reward from stopping.

Their limit v∗v^{*} satisfies the Bellman equations and is the componentwise least feasible vector. It is therefore the unique minimizer of (36).

Define S∗:={j∈A:vj∗=wj}S^{*}:=\{j\in A:v_{j}^{*}=w_{j}\}. At every product outside S∗S^{*}, the Bellman equations give vj∗=∑k∈ℳqj​k​vk∗v_{j}^{*}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{M}}q_{jk}v_{k}^{*}. Repeated substitution expresses vj∗v_{j}^{*} as the expected reward from reaching S∗∪{0}S^{*}\cup\{0\} within finitely many transitions, plus a remainder bounded by WW times the probability of not yet reaching this set. Transience of the product-state submatrix makes the remainder tend to zero. Thus, stopping at the first visit to S∗∪{0}S^{*}\cup\{0\} attains vj∗v_{j}^{*} from every initial product state.

Conversely, any feasible vector of (36) bounds the expected revenue from every assortment contained in AA. It dominates the reward at offered products and the continuation value elsewhere; a finite-step expansion followed by transience gives the corresponding infinite-horizon bound. Starting from the initial distribution λ\lambda, we therefore obtain max⁡∑i∈SS⊆A⁡wi​ϕi​(S)=∑j∈ℳλj​vj∗=∑i∈S∗wi​ϕi​(S∗)\max_{S\subseteq A}\sum_{i\in S}w_{i}\phi_{i}(S)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{M}}\lambda_{j}v_{j}^{*}=\sum_{i\in S^{*}}w_{i}\phi_{i}(S^{*}). Solving (36) and returning S∗S^{*} therefore implements the required oracle, consistent with Blanchet et al. (2016). Products outside AA remain transition states of the chain; they are only ineligible for offering.

The stopping LP has MM variables and at most 2​M2M constraints apart from nonnegativity. For rational inputs, it can be solved exactly in time polynomial in the model input and query size. The value iteration above is used only to prove the characterization; the oracle is computed by solving the LP. The choice probabilities of a returned assortment can also be computed exactly in polynomial time, as shown in Step 3. Applying the oracle to each period therefore provides a polynomial-time strong separation oracle for (35).

Step 3: Establish polynomial solvability. We first verify uniform bounds on the numerical descriptions of the LP coefficients. For an assortment SS, let D=ℳ∖SD=\mathcal{M}\setminus S. Transience implies that I−Qt,D​DI-Q_{t,DD} is nonsingular. Writing λt,D\lambda_{t,D} as a column vector, we have ϕt​i​(S)=λt​i+λt,D𝖳​(I−Qt,D​D)−1​Qt,D​i\phi_{ti}(S)=\lambda_{ti}+\lambda_{t,D}^{\mathsf{T}}(I-Q_{t,DD})^{-1}Q_{t,Di} for i∈Si\in S. The second term is absent when D=∅D=\varnothing. Rational linear algebra and determinant bounds show that these probabilities have encoding length polynomial in MM and LL, uniformly over all assortments. The singleton probabilities at​ia_{ti} can likewise be computed exactly in polynomial time. Thus, every coefficient in the primal and dual has polynomial encoding length, without enumerating the assortments.

The primal is feasible: set all sales variables to zero, offer the empty assortment with probability one, and keep Xt​i(K)=Ci𝟏{K=[1,N]}X_{ti}(K)=C_{i}\mathbf{1}\{K=[1,N]\} throughout the horizon. It is also bounded. Multiplying each interval balance equation by interval length and summing over intervals gives

∑K∈𝒬|K|​Xt+1,i​(K)=∑K∈𝒬|K|​Xt​i​(K)−|It|​∑K∈𝒬Yt​i​(K),t<T.\sum_{K\in\mathcal{Q}}|K|X_{t+1,i}(K)=\sum_{K\in\mathcal{Q}}|K|X_{ti}(K)-|I_{t}|\sum_{K\in\mathcal{Q}}Y_{ti}(K),\hskip 18.49988ptt<T.

Indeed, a feasible cut removes exactly |It||I_{t}| service slots from its parent interval. The initial weighted sum is N​CiNC_{i}, so nonnegativity implies 0≤Xt​i​(K)≤N​Ci0\leq X_{ti}(K)\leq NC_{i}. The choice-mixture and sales-linking constraints also give 0≤∑K∈𝒬Yt​i​(K)=pt​∑S⊆ℳθt​S​ϕt​i​(S)≤pt≤10\leq\sum_{K\in\mathcal{Q}}Y_{ti}(K)=p_{t}\sum_{S\subseteq\mathcal{M}}\theta_{tS}\phi_{ti}(S)\leq p_{t}\leq 1. Together with 0≤θt​S≤10\leq\theta_{tS}\leq 1, these bounds show that the primal has a finite attained optimum. Strong duality therefore applies.

The dual has polynomial dimension, uniformly bounded coefficient encoding lengths, and the strong separation oracle from Step 2. Standard rational-polyhedral bounds also ensure the existence of an optimal dual solution of polynomial encoding length. The rational ellipsoid method consequently computes the optimal value and an optimal dual solution in time polynomial in T,N,M,LT,N,M,L (Grötschel et al. 1981). This exact rational framework also accommodates feasible regions contained in a proper affine subspace.

Step 4: Recover an optimal primal solution and sparse mixtures. The online policy requires the interval flows, so computing the optimal value alone is insufficient. We use the constructive primal-recovery procedure associated with the rational ellipsoid method to identify polynomially many assortment columns that support an optimal primal solution.

To explain why these columns suffice, let R∗R^{*} be the optimal value from Step 3. The primal has polynomially many rows, and all column coefficients have uniformly bounded encoding lengths. A basic feasible solution uses at most as many basic variables as there are rows. Determinant bounds therefore give a computable polynomial bound BB such that every finite optimal value has reduced denominator at most 2B2^{B}, both for the full primal and for any restriction to a subset of its assortment columns. Two distinct such optimal values consequently differ by at least 2−2​B2^{-2B}.

Set ε:=2−2​B−1\varepsilon:=2^{-2B-1}. The dual constraints together with b𝖳​ξ+∑tαt≤R∗−εb^{\mathsf{T}}\xi+\sum_{t}\alpha_{t}\leq R^{*}-\varepsilon form an infeasible rational system. The certificate-producing rational ellipsoid method identifies polynomially many assortment inequalities that, together with the explicit dual constraints and this objective bound, already certify infeasibility. This is the constructive primal-recovery step of the optimization–separation framework (Grötschel et al. 1981).

Any auxiliary bounding box used in this procedure can be chosen uniformly for all relevant subsystems. Indeed, their dimensions and coefficient encoding lengths are polynomially bounded, so every feasible subsystem has a feasible point of polynomial encoding length. A sufficiently large common box therefore preserves feasibility of every such subsystem. Consequently, the infeasibility certificate remains valid after the auxiliary box is removed.

For each period tt, let 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} consist of the assortments appearing in the certificate, together with the empty assortment. Restrict (34) to variables θt​S\theta_{tS} with S∈𝒮tS\in\mathcal{S}_{t}. This restricted primal is feasible because it includes the empty assortment. Its dual retains precisely the corresponding assortment-specific inequalities, together with all explicit dual constraints.

Let R𝒮R_{\mathcal{S}} be the restricted primal optimum. The infeasibility certificate and strong duality imply R𝒮>R∗−εR_{\mathcal{S}}>R^{*}-\varepsilon. Because restricting the available columns cannot increase the primal optimum, R𝒮≤R∗R_{\mathcal{S}}\leq R^{*}. Thus, R∗−ε<R𝒮≤R∗R^{*}-\varepsilon<R_{\mathcal{S}}\leq R^{*}. The rational-value separation bound forces R𝒮=R∗R_{\mathcal{S}}=R^{*}. Solving this polynomial-size restricted primal therefore recovers optimal interval flows and an optimal assortment mixture without enumerating all assortments.

Recover zt​i=(H​u)t​i/ptz_{ti}=(Hu)_{ti}/p_{t}. For each period, we can reduce the mixture support further while holding uu and zz fixed. Over the recovered family 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t}, consider ∑S∈𝒮tθt​S=1\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\theta_{tS}=1, ∑S∈𝒮tθt​S​ϕt​i​(S)=zt​i\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\theta_{tS}\phi_{ti}(S)=z_{ti} for i∈ℳi\in\mathcal{M}, and θt​S≥0\theta_{tS}\geq 0. This system is feasible and bounded. Its equality matrix has rank at most M+1M+1, so a basic feasible solution has at most M+1M+1 positive weights. Such a solution can be obtained by polynomial-time linear programming and basis extraction. Replacing the recovered mixture by this basic solution preserves the purchase probabilities, interval flows, and objective value. We output only its positive weights, with all unlisted assortment weights understood to be zero.

Step 5: Construct the copy-level lift. By Proposition 2, the optimal aggregate solution yields an optimal copy-expanded solution through xt​i​c​(K)=Xt​i​(K)/Cix_{tic}(K)=X_{ti}(K)/C_{i} and yt​i​c​(K)=Yt​i​(K)/Ciy_{tic}(K)=Y_{ti}(K)/C_{i} for c∈[Ci]c\in[C_{i}], with θ\theta and zz unchanged. Writing Ctot:=∑iCiC_{\rm tot}:=\sum_{i}C_{i}, the lift contains 2​T​|𝒬|​Ctot=O⁡(T​N2​Ctot)2T|\mathcal{Q}|C_{\rm tot}=O(TN^{2}C_{\rm tot}) interval entries, each of polynomial encoding length.

Solving the aggregate relaxation takes time polynomial in T,N,M,LT,N,M,L. Explicitly constructing the lift adds a dependence on CtotC_{\rm tot}. Since Ctot≤M​TC_{\rm tot}\leq MT, the full procedure runs in time polynomial in T,N,M,LT,N,M,L, as claimed. ■\blacksquare ∎

D.1 Proof of Lemma 6

Proof.

Proof. Write μ⁡(B):=ℙ⁡(U=B)=∏i∈Bηi​∏i∉B(1−ηi)\mu(B):=\mathbb{P}(U=B)=\prod_{i\in B}\eta_{i}\prod_{i\notin B}(1-\eta_{i}) for B⊆[m]B\subseteq[m]. If m=0m=0, the deterministic pair (J,U)=(0,∅)(J,U)=(0,\varnothing) satisfies the claim. We therefore assume m≥1m\geq 1.

Necessity. The support condition J=i⇒i∈UJ=i\Rightarrow i\in U implies {J∈A}⊆{U∩A≠∅}\{J\in A\}\subseteq\{U\cap A\neq\varnothing\}. Consequently, for every A⊆[m]A\subseteq[m], ∑i∈Aqi≤ℙ⁡(U∩A≠∅)=1−∏i∈A(1−ηi)\sum_{i\in A}q_{i}\leq\mathbb{P}(U\cap A\neq\varnothing)=1-\prod_{i\in A}(1-\eta_{i}).

Sufficiency. Construct a bipartite flow network with a source and a sink. There is a left node for each j∈{0,1,…,m}j\in\{0,1,\ldots,m\}, connected from the source by an edge of capacity qjq_{j}. There is a right node for each B⊆[m]B\subseteq[m], connected to the sink by an edge of capacity μ⁡(B)\mu(B). Connect a left node i>0i>0 to BB whenever i∈Bi\in B, and connect node 00 to every right node. Give these intermediate edges unlimited capacity. The total capacity leaving the source and the total capacity entering the sink both equal one.

For a set AA of left nodes, let N⁡(A)N(A) denote its right neighbors. A finite cut that places exactly AA of the left nodes on the source side must also place N⁡(A)N(A) on that side. The minimum capacity of such a cut is 1−∑j∈Aqj+∑B∈N⁡(A)μ⁡(B)1-\sum_{j\in A}q_{j}+\sum_{B\in N(A)}\mu(B). The max-flow/min-cut theorem therefore gives a flow of value one if and only if ∑j∈Aqj≤∑B∈N⁡(A)μ⁡(B)\sum_{j\in A}q_{j}\leq\sum_{B\in N(A)}\mu(B) for every set AA of left nodes.

If 0∈A0\in A, then N⁡(A)N(A) contains every right node, so its total mass is one and the inequality holds automatically. If 0∉A0\notin A, then N⁡(A)={B:B∩A≠∅}N(A)=\{B:B\cap A\neq\varnothing\}, and the inequality is precisely (26). Thus, the assumed Hall inequalities guarantee a value-one flow.

Such a flow saturates all source and sink capacities. Assigning the flow on edge (j,B)(j,B) as the probability of (J,U)=(j,B)(J,U)=(j,B) gives the prescribed marginals (qj)(q_{j}) and (μ⁡(B))(\mu(B)). The intermediate edges ensure that J=i>0J=i>0 implies i∈Ui\in U.

This network establishes existence. The priority-rule representation below provides a construction that does not enumerate all update sets. ■\blacksquare ∎

The fixed gate γ=1−1/e\gamma=1-1/e introduces an irrational scalar into the purchase probabilities. We compute the priority decomposition through a rational LP and then implement the resulting sampling probabilities exactly.

Thus, only rational LPs need to be solved.

For a purchase outcome J=i>0J=i>0, the posterior weight of a nonempty rule is λh​viπh/qi=μh​viπh/bi\lambda_{h}v_{i}^{\pi^{h}}/q_{i}=\mu_{h}v_{i}^{\pi^{h}}/b_{i}, which is rational. For J=0J=0, write s:=∑ibi≤1s:=\sum_{i}b_{i}\leq 1. The posterior weights of the nonempty rules and the empty rule are, respectively, γ​μh​v0πh/(1−γ​s)\gamma\mu_{h}v_{0}^{\pi^{h}}/(1-\gamma s) and (1−γ​τ)/(1−γ​s)(1-\gamma\tau)/(1-\gamma s). Certified bounds on γ\gamma, and hence on the cumulative sampling probabilities, with error at most 2−k2^{-k} can be computed in time polynomial in kk and the input size. Reveal successive bits of an independent uniform random number and refine these bounds until its dyadic interval is certified to lie between two consecutive cumulative probabilities. Since Ctot≤M​TC_{\rm tot}\leq MT, the full policy therefore runs in expected time polynomial in T,N,MT,N,M and the model input size, with the stated approximation guarantees. Arithmetic-operation counts elsewhere treat random draws as primitive operations.

Proof of Proposition 7. For every outcome jj with qj>0q_{j}>0, the posterior weights are nonnegative and sum to one because ∑h=1Lλh​vjπh=qj\sum_{h=1}^{L}\lambda_{h}v_{j}^{\pi^{h}}=q_{j}. Appendix E Proofs of Results in Section 7

The universal-gate bound is proved in Subsection 7.1. We first establish its sharpness and the lossless MNL coupling, then verify the MNL assortment oracle, copy-update law, and state invariants. We prove the two approximation guarantees together and give their associated MNL tightness result, followed by the stronger zero-outside-option guarantee.

E.1 Proof of Proposition 9

Proof.

Proof. Step 1: Construct the choice and update probabilities. For m≥1m\geq 1, let the customer start uniformly on mm product states, each of which transitions directly to the outside option. Then ϕi​(S)=1/m\phi_{i}(S)=1/m for i∈Si\in S and ai=1/ma_{i}=1/m. The product-state submatrix is zero and therefore transient.

Take p=1p=1, select S=[m]S=[m], and suppose one copy of each product proposes. The gated purchase probabilities sum to γ\gamma. Each proposed copy is updated with probability 1/m1/m, independently under the target law. Thus, the probability of at least one update is gm:=1−(1−1m)mg_{m}:=1-\left(1-\frac{1}{m}\right)^{m}.

Step 2: Apply the Hall inequality. The Hall condition for A=[m]A=[m] requires γ≤gm\gamma\leq g_{m}. Since gm→1−1/eg_{m}\to 1-1/e, any fixed γ∈(1−1/e,1]\gamma\in(1-1/e,1] violates this condition for sufficiently large mm. The required coupling then does not exist.

Step 3: Realize the proposal profile in a nonterminal period. First consider a one-period instance with one service slot, one initially free copy per product, and unit revenues. The full-assortment SBLP solution has zi=ai=1/mz_{i}=a_{i}=1/m and objective one. It is optimal because the total purchase probability cannot exceed one. Its proposal probabilities are ρi=zi/ai=1\rho_{i}=z_{i}/a_{i}=1, so every copy proposes.

To make this period nonterminal, append a second request for the same service slot, with the same arrival and choice parameters and zero revenues. The interval balances give x2,i,1​([1,1])=1−1/mx_{2,i,1}([1,1])=1-1/m. In the second period, select the empty assortment and set all sales flows to zero. This extends the first-period solution to a feasible SBLP solution of value one. It remains optimal because the second period generates no revenue.

The first period therefore realizes the stated proposal profile with probability one. With unit revenues, the assortment oracle selects all products, so the Hall obstruction arises within the online construction. Together with Proposition 8, this proves sharpness among uniform scalar gates. ■\blacksquare ∎

E.3 Efficient MNL Assortment Optimization

Consider a candidate set AA, nonnegative product weights wiw_{i}, and positive outside attractiveness normalized to one. Write Rw​(S):=∑i∈Swi​ui1+∑i∈SuiR_{w}(S):=\frac{\sum_{i\in S}w_{i}u_{i}}{1+\sum_{i\in S}u_{i}} and R∗:=maxS⊆A⁡Rw​(S)R^{*}:=\max_{S\subseteq A}R_{w}(S). For j∈A∖Sj\in A\setminus S, adding product jj changes the objective by

Rw​(S∪{j})−Rw​(S)=uj​(wj−Rw​(S))1+∑i∈Sui+uj.R_{w}(S\cup\{j\})-R_{w}(S)=\frac{u_{j}(w_{j}-R_{w}(S))}{1+\sum_{i\in S}u_{i}+u_{j}}.

For j∈Sj\in S, removing it changes the objective by

Rw​(S∖{j})−Rw​(S)=uj​(Rw​(S)−wj)1+∑i∈Sui−uj.R_{w}(S\setminus\{j\})-R_{w}(S)=\frac{u_{j}(R_{w}(S)-w_{j})}{1+\sum_{i\in S}u_{i}-u_{j}}.

At an optimum, every product with wi>R∗w_{i}>R^{*} must be included, and every product with wi<R∗w_{i}<R^{*} must be excluded. Products with wi=R∗w_{i}=R^{*} can be added without changing the objective. Thus, an optimal assortment can be chosen as a prefix of the products ordered by nonincreasing weight.

After sorting, cumulative sums of uiu_{i} and wi​uiw_{i}u_{i} allow all prefixes to be evaluated in linear time. Including the empty assortment, the oracle requires O⁡(|A|​log⁡|A|)O(|A|\log|A|) arithmetic and comparison operations; an empty candidate set is handled directly. This implements both the actual-revenue oracle and the nonnegative weighted queries used in solving the SBLP.

Proof.

Write Xi=(Xi​1,…,Xi​mi)X_{i}=(X_{i1},\ldots,X_{im_{i}}), and let Li​(bi∣ui)L_{i}(b_{i}\mid u_{i}) denote its conditional lifting law, with arbitrary values on conditioning events of probability zero. =∏i∈Ptνi​(bi).\displaystyle=\prod_{i\in P_{t}}\nu_{i}(b_{i}).

The first equality uses independence of the product-level indicators and independent lifting conditional on them. The final equality follows from Step 1. Since each νi\nu_{i} is itself a Bernoulli product law, the resulting joint distribution factors over all proposed copies.

Step 3: Sample a nonempty copy vector directly. For 0<αi<10<\alpha_{i}<1 and Ui=1U_{i}=1, draw the position of the first success according to

ℙ⁡(Ki=k∣Ui=1)=αi​(1−αi)k−1ηi,k∈[mi].\mathbb{P}(K_{i}=k\mid U_{i}=1)=\frac{\alpha_{i}(1-\alpha_{i})^{k-1}}{\eta_{i}},\hskip 18.49988ptk\in[m_{i}].

Set all coordinates before KiK_{i} to zero, set coordinate KiK_{i} to one, and sample the remaining coordinates independently as Bernoulli(αi)(\alpha_{i}). For any nonzero vector bb, multiplying the first-success probability by the probabilities of its remaining coordinates gives νi​(b)/ηi\nu_{i}(b)/\eta_{i}, as required.

If αi=1\alpha_{i}=1, the vector is deterministically all ones. If αi=0\alpha_{i}=0, the branch Ui=1U_{i}=1 never occurs. The construction requires O⁡(mi)O(m_{i}) arithmetic operations and random draws, without a rejection step whose cost depends on ηi\eta_{i}. ■\blacksquare ∎

E.5 Proof of Theorem 3

Proof.

Proof. Fix the SBLP solution used by the policy. We prove the virtual-state properties by induction using the joint transition law, and establish physical feasibility along each sample path. The terminal period is treated separately.

Step 1: Initialize the induction. At t=1t=1, every actual and virtual free-slot set equals the deterministic set 𝒩\mathcal{N}. Thus, virtual availability is contained in actual availability, the interval marginals satisfy (11), and the virtual states are independent across copies.

Let BkB_{k} denote copy kk’s proposal indicator. Its conditional proposal probability βk​(Fk)\beta_{k}(F_{k}) equals πt​i​c​(K)\pi_{tic}(K) if FkF_{k} has a maximal free interval KK containing ItI_{t}, and equals zero otherwise. Conditional on FF, the proposal indicators are independent, with ℙ⁡(Bk=1∣F)=βk​(Fk)\mathbb{P}(B_{k}=1\mid F)=\beta_{k}(F_{k}).

Let DkD_{k} indicate whether copy kk receives a virtual cut, and write αk:=pt​at​i\alpha_{k}:=p_{t}a_{ti} for k=(i,c)k=(i,c). A nonproposed copy is never cut. For a proposed copy, Lemma 7 gives the target Bernoulli update law after averaging over the gate and customer outcome. Thus, ℙ⁡(D=d∣F,B=b)=∏kLk​(dk∣bk)\mathbb{P}(D=d\mid F,B=b)=\prod_{k}L_{k}(d_{k}\mid b_{k}), where Lk​(1∣0)=0L_{k}(1\mid 0)=0, Lk​(0∣0)=1L_{k}(0\mid 0)=1, Lk​(1∣1)=αkL_{k}(1\mid 1)=\alpha_{k}, and Lk​(0∣1)=1−αkL_{k}(0\mid 1)=1-\alpha_{k}. The lemma holds for every preselected assortment, and this product law does not depend on which assortment is selected. The identity therefore also holds if the assortment oracle randomizes among maximizers.

Each LkL_{k} depends on the proposal profile only through bkb_{k}. Averaging over the independent proposals consequently gives

ℙ⁡(D=d∣F)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(D=d\mid F) =∑b∈{0,1}Ctot∏kℙ⁡(Bk=bk∣Fk)​Lk​(dk∣bk)\displaystyle=\sum_{b\in\{0,1\}^{C_{\rm tot}}}\prod_{k}\mathbb{P}(B_{k}=b_{k}\mid F_{k})L_{k}(d_{k}\mid b_{k})
=∏k∑bk∈{0,1}ℙ⁡(Bk=bk∣Fk)​Lk​(dk∣bk).\displaystyle=\prod_{k}\sum_{b_{k}\in\{0,1\}}\mathbb{P}(B_{k}=b_{k}\mid F_{k})L_{k}(d_{k}\mid b_{k}).

Hence, the cut indicators are independent conditional on FF, with success probabilities δk​(Fk):=βk​(Fk)​αk\delta_{k}(F_{k}):=\beta_{k}(F_{k})\alpha_{k}. For a virtually feasible copy whose containing maximal interval is KK, δk​(Fk)=πt​i​c​(K)​pt​at​i=yt​i​c​(K)xt​i​c​(K)=κt​i​c​(K)\delta_{k}(F_{k})=\pi_{tic}(K)p_{t}a_{ti}=\frac{y_{tic}(K)}{x_{tic}(K)}=\kappa_{tic}(K), using the zero-ratio convention when xt​i​c​(K)=0x_{tic}(K)=0. Virtually infeasible copies have zero cut probability.

Step 3: Preserve independence and interval marginals. The next virtual state of copy kk is Fk∖ItF_{k}\setminus I_{t} if Dk=1D_{k}=1, and FkF_{k} otherwise. Its transition therefore depends only on its own current state, and the joint transition kernel factors across copies.

Let Kk​(Fk′∣Fk)K_{k}(F^{\prime}_{k}\mid F_{k}) denote this one-copy transition kernel and μt,k\mu_{t,k} the current one-copy state distribution. Independence at the beginning of period tt then gives

=∏k∑Fkμt,k​(Fk)​Kk​(Fk′∣Fk).\displaystyle=\prod_{k}\sum_{F_{k}}\mu_{t,k}(F_{k})K_{k}(F^{\prime}_{k}\mid F_{k}).

This proves independence at the next period boundary. The local transition agrees with Lemma 5, so it also preserves the prescribed interval marginals xt+1,i,c​(K)x_{t+1,i,c}(K).

Iterating this argument establishes properties (iii) and (iv) through the beginning of period TT. These distributional statements average over past outcomes; they do not condition on a realized purchase history.

Step 4: Preserve physical feasibility and state inclusion. Suppose virtual availability is contained in actual availability at the beginning of period t<Tt<T. Every proposed copy then satisfies It⊆ℱ¯t​i​c⊆ℱt​i​cI_{t}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{F}}_{tic}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{tic}, so it can physically fulfill the request.

If Jt=iJ_{t}=i, the coupling gives Ut​i=1U_{ti}=1, and the lifting ensures Wt​i≠∅W_{ti}\neq\varnothing. The policy assigns the purchase to one copy c∗∈Wt​ic^{*}\in W_{ti}. Every other updated copy loses ItI_{t} only from its virtual set, and all remaining copies are unchanged. If Jt=0J_{t}=0, the actual sets remain unchanged and the virtual sets can only shrink.

Thus, each nonterminal period preserves virtual containment, and every purchase reserves the requested interval on exactly one physically feasible copy.

Step 5: Complete the terminal period. At the beginning of period TT, the preceding induction has established all state properties. Any purchased product belongs to the visible set and therefore has a proposed, physically feasible copy. The terminal rule assigns the purchase to one such copy and removes the requested interval from both its actual and virtual sets.

This establishes physical feasibility throughout the horizon and virtual containment through period boundary T+1T+1. No prescribed interval marginals or independence property at T+1T+1 are required, completing the proof. ■\blacksquare ∎

E.6 Proof of Theorem 1

Proof.

Proof. Let π\pi denote Algorithm 1 with the exact assortment oracle for the relevant choice model and gate probability γ\gamma in every nonterminal period. Theorem 3 establishes feasibility and ensures that the static extraction bound applies in every period.

Set Wt:=∑i∈ℳrt​i​zt​iW_{t}:=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{M}}r_{ti}z_{ti}, and let PtP_{t} denote the visible product set in period tt. By Corollary 1, 𝔼⁡[ft​(Pt)]≥Wt/2\mathbb{E}[f_{t}(P_{t})]\geq W_{t}/2. The coupling preserves the purchase probabilities induced by the selected gate, and the terminal period requires no gate. Multiplying by the arrival probabilities and summing over periods therefore gives

Vπ​(I)\displaystyle V^{\pi}(I) =γ​∑t<Tpt​𝔼​[ft​(Pt)]+pT​𝔼​[fT​(PT)]\displaystyle=\gamma\sum_{t<T}p_{t}\mathbb{E}[f_{t}(P_{t})]+p_{T}\mathbb{E}[f_{T}(P_{T})]
≥12​(γ​∑t<Tpt​Wt+pT​WT)\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}\left(\gamma\sum_{t<T}p_{t}W_{t}+p_{T}W_{T}\right)
≥γ2​∑t=1Tpt​Wt=γ2​SBLPMCC⁡(I).\displaystyle\geq\frac{\gamma}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}p_{t}W_{t}=\frac{\gamma}{2}\operatorname{SBLP}_{\rm MC}^{C}(I).

The final inequality uses 0≤γ≤10\leq\gamma\leq 1 and nonnegative revenues.

Under general Markov chain choice, Proposition 8 makes the coupling feasible with γ=1−1/e\gamma=1-1/e, giving VπMC​(I)≥(1−1/e)​SBLPMCC⁡(I)/2V^{\pi_{\rm MC}}(I)\geq(1-1/e)\operatorname{SBLP}_{\rm MC}^{C}(I)/2. Under MNL, Proposition 10 permits γ=1\gamma=1, giving VπMNL​(I)≥SBLPMCC⁡(I)/2V^{\pi_{\rm MNL}}(I)\geq\operatorname{SBLP}_{\rm MC}^{C}(I)/2. Since the SBLP upper-bounds Von​(I)V^{\rm on}(I), these inequalities establish (3) and (4), respectively.

The relaxation, assortment optimization, and priority decompositions are computable in polynomial time. Our convention Ci≤TC_{i}\leq T gives Ctot≤M​TC_{\rm tot}\leq MT, so maintaining individual copies also requires polynomial space and time. The required random draws admit exact implementations with expected polynomial running time, as detailed in Appendix D.3. ■\blacksquare ∎

E.7 Proof of Proposition 11

Proof.

Proof. For each m≥2m\geq 2, take the MNL choice model constructed in Appendix B.1 and form an instance ℐm\mathcal{I}_{m} with one booking period, one service slot, arrival probability one, and one physical copy per product. Let WmW_{m} denote the full-assortment revenue, and let PmP_{m} and fmf_{m} denote the independent candidate set and optimal assortment-revenue function from that construction. Since revenue is strictly increasing in assortment size, the full assortment is the unique optimal offer, and Von​(ℐm)=WmV^{\mathrm{on}}(\mathcal{I}_{m})=W_{m}.

Suppressing the period and copy indices, the full-assortment mixture induces the feasible SBLP solution

xi​([1,1])=1,yi​([1,1])=zi=ϕi​(ℳ).x_{i}([1,1])=1,\hskip 18.49988pty_{i}([1,1])=z_{i}=\phi_{i}(\mathcal{M}).

The state-capacity constraint holds because zi≤aiz_{i}\leq a_{i}. Every feasible SBLP objective is a convex combination of assortment revenues and therefore cannot exceed WmW_{m}. Strict optimality of the full assortment forces every optimal mixture to assign it weight one. With one copy and one service interval per product, the sales flows are consequently unique.

The policy therefore proposes each product independently with probability

yi​([1,1])ai​xi​([1,1])=ziai,\frac{y_{i}([1,1])}{a_{i}x_{i}([1,1])}=\frac{z_{i}}{a_{i}},

so its visible set has exactly the law of PmP_{m}, regardless of how an optimal SBLP solution is selected. The single period is ungated, and the assortment oracle earns fm​(Pm)f_{m}(P_{m}) in conditional expectation. Hence,

VπMNL​(ℐm)Von​(ℐm)=𝔼​[fm​(Pm)]Wm⟶12,\frac{V^{\pi_{\mathrm{MNL}}}(\mathcal{I}_{m})}{V^{\mathrm{on}}(\mathcal{I}_{m})}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[f_{m}(P_{m})]}{W_{m}}\longrightarrow\frac{1}{2},

where the limit was established in Appendix B.1. The first member ℐ1\mathcal{I}_{1} may be any admissible one-period, unit-capacity MNL instance with positive optimal revenue. ■\blacksquare ∎

E.8 Verification of Remark 3

Proof.

Proof. Step 1: Define the boundary choice model. Fix a period and suppress its index. With zero outside-option attractiveness and ui>0u_{i}>0 for every product, define

The denominator is used only when i∈Si\in S, so it is positive. Every nonempty assortment has total purchase probability one, and ai=1a_{i}=1. Regularity follows directly from the choice formula.

The revenue of a nonempty assortment is an attractiveness-weighted average of its product revenues. Consequently, f⁡(A)=maxi∈A⁡rif(A)=\max_{i\in A}r_{i} for A≠∅A\neq\varnothing, with f⁡(∅)=0f(\varnothing)=0; a highest-revenue singleton attains this value.

≥1−exp(−∑i∈Aτ∑c=1Ciρi​c)\displaystyle\geq 1-\exp\!\left(-\sum_{i\in A_{\tau}}\sum_{c=1}^{C_{i}}\rho_{ic}\right)
=1−e−Zτ≥(1−1e)​Zτ.\displaystyle=1-e^{-Z_{\tau}}\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)Z_{\tau}.

The first inequality uses 1−u≤e−u1-u\leq e^{-u}; the last follows from concavity of 1−e−z1-e^{-z} on [0,1][0,1]. Integrating over revenue thresholds yields

≥(1−1e)​∫0∞Zτ​dτ=(1−1e)​∑iri​zi.\displaystyle\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)\int_{0}^{\infty}Z_{\tau}\,d\tau=\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)\sum_{i}r_{i}z_{i}.

This bound holds for arbitrary copy multiplicities and does not require the copy-level flows to be symmetric.

Step 3: Verify the coupling and online guarantee. For every arrival probability p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1] and nonempty A⊆SA\subseteq S, 1−∏i∈A(1−p​ai)=1−(1−p)|A|≥p≥p​∑i∈Aϕi​(S)1-\prod_{i\in A}(1-pa_{i})=1-(1-p)^{|A|}\geq p\geq p\sum_{i\in A}\phi_{i}(S). The empty-subset inequality is automatic. Hence, all Hall conditions hold with γ=1\gamma=1; additional proposed copies only increase the update coverage.

The SBLP upper-bound and interval-flow arguments remain valid for these regular choice probabilities and singleton bounds. The posterior sampler and copy-level lifting reproduce the prescribed independent update law, so the induction in Theorem 3 also applies. Thus, the proposal distribution used in Step 2 is maintained in every period, and every purchase is physically feasible.

Restoring the time index, set Wt:=∑irt​i​zt​iW_{t}:=\sum_{i}r_{ti}z_{ti}. If every period has zero outside-option attractiveness, all periods are ungated and the stronger static bound gives

VπMNL​(I)\displaystyle V^{\pi_{\rm MNL}}(I) =∑t=1Tpt​𝔼​[ft​(Pt)]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}p_{t}\mathbb{E}[f_{t}(P_{t})]
≥(1−1e)​∑t=1Tpt​Wt=(1−1e)​SBLPMCC⁡(I)≥(1−1e)​Von​(I).\displaystyle\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)\sum_{t=1}^{T}p_{t}W_{t}=\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)\operatorname{SBLP}_{\rm MC}^{C}(I)\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)V^{\rm on}(I).

Step 4: Verify tractability and the scope of the improvement. For arbitrary signed product weights, a singleton attaining the largest positive eligible weight is optimal. If no eligible weight is positive, the empty assortment is optimal. This provides a polynomial-time weighted assortment oracle. The aggregate relaxation, symmetric lift, and conditional sampling procedures therefore remain tractable.

If positive and zero outside-option attractiveness occur in different periods, the same policy remains feasible. Its period-level extraction factor is 1−1/e1-1/e in each zero-outside period and 1/21/2 in each positive-outside period. In particular, the general 1/21/2 guarantee still holds in this mixed setting; the uniform 1−1/e1-1/e guarantee above concerns instances with zero outside-option attractiveness in every period. ■\blacksquare ∎

Tightness under the symmetric lift. Consider T=CT=C booking periods, one service slot, and one product with CC copies. In every period, arrival is certain, the request is for the single service slot, and the outside option has zero attractiveness. Revenue is one in the first period and zero in all remaining periods. Every optimal SBLP solution has first-period sales probability one, so the symmetric lift assigns first-period proposal probability 1/C1/C to each copy. The policy’s expected revenue is therefore 1−(1−1/C)C1-(1-1/C)^{C}, whereas Von​(I)=1V^{\rm on}(I)=1. The ratio approaches 1−1/e1-1/e as C→∞C\to\infty, showing that the factor is tight for the policy using the symmetric lift.
